docs.title: Writing conventions
docs.text:
• One file per concept. If you find yourself writing "see also…" to the same page three times, that page should be split or linked from the index instead.
  • Code blocks are triple-backtick fenced with a language tag so GitHub + mkdocs highlight them.
  • Internal links are relative paths from the current file — nothing absolute.
  • Line length is wrap-at-will — prose, not code — because Markdown re-wraps on render and short lines show up as awkward in some viewers.
  • No emoji in headings. Rendering is spotty on some platforms.
  • Every doc has a "last reviewed" footer when it covers something version-dependent. Stub docs that haven't been reviewed yet say so in italics at the top.

docs.title: Building the docs as a site
docs.text:
The docs ship as plain Markdown; if you want them as a navigable site, mkdocs-material will render the same files unchanged:

pip install mkdocs-material
mkdocs serve        # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000
mkdocs build        # static site under site/

A minimal mkdocs.yml ships in the repo root. We don't publish to GitHub Pages yet — flip the switch in Settings → Pages when the time comes.

docs.title: Does this root my Quest?
docs.text: No. It doesn't modify any system file, doesn't require USB debugging after the first install, and can't elevate past what Android gives any sideloaded app on your device. It's a normal APK. Uninstalling it leaves the system identical to how it was.

docs.title: Can it remove Facebook/Meta integration?
docs.text:
No — and any app that claims to on a locked-bootloader Quest 2 is lying or malware. The Meta apps live on a dm-verity-signed partition; removing them changes the partition's Merkle tree, which breaks vbmeta_system verification, and the bootloader refuses to continue. We explain the full chain in reverse-engineering/avb-chain.md.

What QuestClassic does do is give you a visible map of the Meta online stack and let you verify your own OTAs offline — knowledge, not removal.

docs.title: Does the self-updater talk to Meta?
docs.text:
No. It polls one host — api.github.com — and downloads release APKs from github.com. That's the entire network footprint of the self-updater. The AI Companion panel talks to whatever provider YOU configured (and only if you configured one).

Full list of network endpoints the app can reach is in security/model.md.

docs.title: Will it survive Meta's OTAs?
docs.text: Yes. Meta's A/B OTAs don't wipe user-installed APKs; QuestClassic + its DataStore persist through every HorizonOS update. The one exception: a factory reset wipes user data and you'd need to reinstall. See architecture/storage.md for storage details.

docs.title: Why doesn't the "three-lines boot menu" idea work?
docs.text: That's a bootloader-level interaction. QuestClassic is an Android app — init finishes booting the OS before the first app runs. We never see the boot key combo and can't intercept it. The bootloader is itself signed, so even flashing a replacement is impossible on a locked device. See reverse-engineering/avb-chain.md.

docs.title: Can I write my own panels?
docs.text: Yes. contributing/getting-started.md walks through adding a panel in ~30 lines. Each existing panel under app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ui/panels/ is a self-contained example.

docs.title: Why 90° for the AR hand menu?
docs.text: Research on wrist-anchored menus — Meta published some of this in 2023 — shows 90° is the sweet spot across most adults' comfortable wrist-rotation range. Larger arcs force uncomfortable supination; smaller ones crowd the tiles. See user-guide/ar-home.md.

docs.title: Does it work on Quest 3 / Quest Pro?
docs.text: The supported-devices allow-list in AndroidManifest.xml includes hollywood (Quest 2), monterey (Quest Pro), panther (Quest 3S), eureka (Quest 3), seacliff (reserved). It should work; Quest 3-specific features (depth sensor, Quest 3 controllers) aren't surfaced yet but nothing in the current app depends on Quest-2-specific hardware either.

docs.title: Is this legal?
docs.text: Modifying your own device, writing apps for it, reading its OS from userspace APIs, and publishing APKs to GitHub — yes, universally legal. Reverse-engineering for interoperability is explicitly permitted under DMCA §1201(f) in the US and under similar clauses in EU/UK/AU law. We do not distribute Meta's copyrighted binaries or decompiled source; see the README's "Legal / IP posture".

docs.title: What if Meta changes their OTA format?
docs.text: The Signature Verifier reads the CrAU header version and falls back gracefully; if Meta moved to a new format, the panel would say "unsupported version" rather than silently producing wrong results. We'd then write a new verifier against the new format. The reverse-engineering notes are in this repo precisely so that's reproducible.

docs.title: Can I use a Meta account to sign in via QuestClassic?
docs.text: No — QuestClassic doesn't do account auth. All it does is help you see the Meta auth flow (via the Meta Hosts Audit + System Internals panels). If an app ever asks you for your Meta password, that is NOT one of ours. The AI Companion panel asks for an AI-provider API key (Anthropic / OpenAI / your Ollama URL) — that's it.

docs.title: How do I earn the GitHub achievements?
docs.text: See contributing/achievements.md. Everything legitimate; no fake accounts, no star rings.

docs.title: I found a security issue, who do I tell?
docs.text: See security/reporting.md. Short version: don't open a public issue; use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting flow on the repo.

docs.title: ADR 0001 — Record architecture decisions
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text: We want future contributors to know why we made the technical choices we made, so they don't spend time reversing-engineer intent or re-litigating settled decisions.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We adopt Michael Nygard's "Architecture Decision Records" convention. Each non-trivial technical decision gets a numbered ADR in docs/adr/. ADRs are immutable — if we change our mind later, we write a new ADR that supersedes the old one, we don't edit the old one.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Title · status · date
Context — what forced this decision
Decision — what we decided
Consequences — what this makes easier + harder

Short. No padding. If an ADR needs more than two screens, it's probably actually two decisions.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: readers can trace "why does the DI container look like this?" to ADR 0003 rather than guessing.
  • +: a fresh maintainer can read docs/adr/*.md and know the whole set of commitments the project has made.
  • -: writing an ADR adds overhead to a PR that makes a significant decision. We accept this.

docs.title: ADR 0002 — Use Jetpack Compose for all UI
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We're building a 2D panel app for Quest that runs as a sideloaded APK. Options:

  1. Classic Android Views (XML layouts + View/ViewGroup).
  2. Jetpack Compose.
  3. Unity (overkill — this is a 2D panel app, not a VR game).
  4. Flutter (great cross-platform story we don't need; adds a Dart runtime).
  5. React Native (adds a JS runtime + bridge; complexity we don't need).

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Jetpack Compose for 100% of UI. No XML layouts, no Views, no Fragments beyond what Compose uses internally.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• First-party Android UI toolkit, actively developed.
  • The declarative model fits our "single HomeScreen enum + when dispatch" navigation perfectly.
  • Interop with the Android platform is excellent — Activities, Intents, PackageManager work exactly the same.
  • No bridge / no runtime beyond what we already need (Kotlin stdlib + coroutines).
  • The nostalgic Oculus look is easy to implement with Compose primitives (gradients, Canvas, custom shapes) and would be painful to retrofit from XML.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: fast UI iteration, hot-reload via Compose Preview when we want it.
  • +: smaller APK than Compose + XML + Views stack.
  • +: Compose Multiplatform story (if we ever want desktop/iOS) is open.
  • -: Compose has a learning curve for Android developers who've only done XML.
  • -: Some rare Android widgets don't have Compose equivalents yet (we haven't hit one).

docs.title: ADR 0003 — Hand-wired DI, no runtime DI library
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We need a way to construct and share repositories (AppList, Haptics, Diagnostics, PayloadVerifier, AI, Update, …) across panels. Options:

  1. Hilt (Dagger wrapper for Android).
  2. Dagger (plain).
  3. Koin (DSL-based service locator).
  4. Anvil (Dagger + Compose-friendly).
  5. Hand-wired: one class that holds all the dependencies as vals.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: Hand-wired: app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/core/AppContainer.kt, a single class constructed in QuestClassicApplication.onCreate().

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• The dependency graph is tiny. 9 repositories, no scoping concerns, no per-Activity-or-Fragment dependencies.
  • Hilt/Dagger would add ~1 s of build-time annotation processing (KAPT) or KSP overhead, plus generated-code indirection when reading.
  • Koin would add a runtime service-locator pattern where missing bindings fail at first-read at runtime instead of compile-time.
  • Hand-wired is compile-time-verified, instant to read ("what exists? look at AppContainer"), zero-overhead at runtime, and has no toolchain footprint.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text:
We'll reconsider adopting Hilt when any of these happens:

  • The graph passes 20 bindings.
  • We need per-user or per-Activity scoping (real AR mode with a SpatialActivity session might trigger this).
  • We split into multiple Gradle modules.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: faster build (no annotation processing).
  • +: new contributors read one Kotlin class and know the whole graph.
  • +: no runtime surprises (compile errors beat crashes-on-first-read).
  • -: if we outgrow it, the migration to Hilt is a day of work. We accept the one-time cost later for the ongoing simplicity now.

docs.title: ADR 0004 — No telemetry, ever
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Modern Android apps routinely bundle analytics (Firebase, Mixpanel, Amplitude, Google Analytics), crash reporting (Crashlytics, Sentry), remote config (Firebase Remote Config), and more. Each one phones home.

QuestClassic's entire point is to be a tool its users trust — sitting next to Meta's heavily-telemetered stack, running on a device whose user may have specifically sought us out because they don't want more analytics on their headset.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Zero telemetry. No analytics SDK. No crash-reporting SDK that phones home by default. No remote config. No "anonymous usage metrics." No A/B testing harness.

The app phones home to exactly two hosts, and only when the user engages with specific features:

Host Trigger Content api.github.com Open Updates panel GET /releases/latest github.com Tap "Install" in Updates GET the release's APK

Plus whichever AI provider the user configured, if any. And DNS-lookups + ICMP pings to the 24 Meta hosts if the user opens the Meta Hosts Audit panel — but nothing is POSTed to those.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• Users who install a sideloaded app sometimes do so BECAUSE they want less telemetry.
  • Our features don't need analytics to improve — we read PRs and issues.
  • Crash reporting we don't have is handled by users reporting bugs with the buzz pattern that fired + a logcat excerpt.
  • Trust is cheap to lose and expensive to earn back.

docs.title: What's NOT banned
docs.text:
• Opt-in crash reporting (Sentry, Bugsnag, etc.) — some day, if a user explicitly turns it on, and it's clearly disclosed. Not on by default. Not v0.1.0.
  • Local logging (our own stuff written to /data/data/*/files) — fine; doesn't leave the device.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: easy promise to make ("we don't phone home"); easy to verify (grep the manifest for INTERNET-using classes, there aren't many).
  • +: smaller APK, faster start, no init-chain surprises.
  • +: this ADR exists so no one accidentally adds Firebase without noticing it's a policy break.
  • -: we won't have built-in feature-usage data. We'll have to rely on PRs and issues for signal. We accept this.

docs.title: ADR 0005 — GitHub Releases as the update channel
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
We need to ship updates to installed users. On a sideloaded Android app we can't go through Google Play, we can't go through Meta's Store (Oculus/Horizon Store requires Meta vendor status), and we can't piggyback on Meta's OTA (requires a key we don't have and never will — see reverse-engineering/avb-chain.md).

Options:

  1. Host the APK on a server we run; the app polls a URL for new versions.
  2. Use F-Droid.
  3. Use GitHub Releases.
  4. Don't ship updates; tell users to manually redownload.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: GitHub Releases as the primary update channel for v0.1.0.

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• Free. We'd otherwise need a static server.
  • Reliable. GitHub's CDN is what pretty much every piece of open-source infra relies on.
  • Discoverable. Users already go to the repo for everything else.
  • One api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/releases/latest call gets us version + asset list in one trip.
  • Signing is orthogonal — we can self-sign the APK (see security/signing.md) and attach it to the release.
  • Forks work for free — the CI workflow sed-rewrites owner/repo at release time, so a fork gets its own channel.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text:
• When a maintainer wants F-Droid listing. Not blocked by us; they can set it up alongside GitHub Releases.
  • When GitHub's rate limits start affecting us (unlikely at any imaginable scale for this app).
  • If GitHub ever changes its terms in a way that makes this unworkable. We'd mirror.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: free, reliable, discoverable, self-service for forks.
  • +: no infra to run.
  • -: we don't currently publish release signatures in a way that's cryptographically verifiable beyond GitHub's own HTTPS. Signing the APK itself is the fix (tracked in issue #11).
  • -: GitHub may rate-limit or geo-block. We fail-soft: the Updates panel says "couldn't reach" and that's it.

docs.title: ADR 0006 — Depend on material-icons-extended
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07
  • Supersedes: n/a
  • Related: this ADR was prompted by a CI failure where the base material-icons-core was too narrow for our palette.

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Jetpack Compose ships two icon libraries:

  • material-icons-core — a few dozen commonly-used icons.
  • material-icons-extended — the full Material Icons set, ~2000 icons, adds ~250 KB to the APK.

We use Icons.Outlined.{Apps, Chat, MonitorHeart, CloudDownload, Info, Verified, Policy, Public, ViewInAr, Build}. Several of those live only in extended.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Depend on material-icons-extended. One line in app/build.gradle.kts:

implementation(libs.androidx.compose.material.icons.extended)

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• Icon choice is a UX decision; forcing the designer to use only the core set would bloat panels with awkward icon choices OR require shipping vector drawables ourselves (which costs the same APK bytes).
  • Extended is first-party; it's not an extra dependency source.
  • 250 KB is a rounding error on an app that'll land around 2.5 MB total.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: unrestricted icon choice.
  • +: future panels don't have to think about which bucket an icon lives in.
  • -: 250 KB APK bloat. Acceptable.

docs.title: ADR 0007 — minSdk = 29 to match Quest 2's first API level
docs.text:
• Status: Accepted
  • Date: 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Android's minSdk tells Android which devices CAN install the app. Too low means we can't use modern APIs without guarding. Too high excludes devices we'd otherwise support.

We reverse-engineered the Quest 2 OTA and found:

  • ro.product.first_api_level = 29 on Quest 2 (= Android 10).
  • Current userdevice: Android 14 (SDK 34), HorizonOS branch releases-oculus-14.0-v209.
  • Quest Pro / Quest 3 / Quest 3S all run Android 14 base too.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
• minSdk = 29 (matching Quest 2's first API level).
  • targetSdk = 35 (Android 15; required for core-ktx:1.15.0 which we use).
  • compileSdk = 35 (same).

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
• minSdk 29 covers every Quest ever made that runs modern HorizonOS.
  • minSdk 29 covers ~98% of Android devices in the wild, so we don't lose non-Quest users who might want the app on a regular Android tablet.
  • Dropping to 24 or lower would gain nothing (no earlier Quest supports HorizonOS anyway) and cost us the deprecations.
  • Going higher than 29 would exclude Quest 2 users whose device still reports first_api_level=29.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• +: we can freely use anything from API 29 (notification channels, scoped storage, wi-fi suggestion API, the works).
  • +: no @TargetApi guards for the common case.
  • -: API 29+ shuns some older patterns (scoped storage, implicit broadcast limits). We don't do anything that trips on this.

docs.title: When to revisit
docs.text:
• If a user reports they're on a Quest-1-era HorizonOS that's still API 28 or lower (very unlikely — Quest 1 is end-of-life).
  • When targetSdk bumps become non-trivial (core-ktx and friends will push us to 36, 37 over time).

docs.title: ADR 0008 — AR semicircle hand menu uses a 90° arc, not a radial ring
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The Quest hand-tracking API delivers 26 joint poses per hand at ~60 Hz. The question is how to lay out an "app menu" around the hand so the user can select with the other hand without first learning a gesture vocabulary.

Three options we considered:

  1. Radial ring — a full 360° circle around the palm. Looks slick in demos; miserable for selection because half the slots sit inside your arm.
  2. Vertical stack — a floating column above the palm. Easy, but it eats a lot of vertical FOV and the farthest slot is 40° above neutral gaze.
  3. 90° arc — a quarter-circle fan pointing away from the body, across a horizontal plane. Natural ergonomics, no "inside the arm" slots, all slots in the comfortable 20° cone around the gaze normal.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text: We ship the 90° semicircle, swept from −45° to +45° around the hand-pointer's world-space forward vector, at a radius of 15 cm from the palm center.

docs.title: Geometry details
docs.text:
• Pivot: midpoint of the thumb MCP and pinky MCP joints (the "palm center" pseudo-joint).
  • Arc plane: the plane normal to the vector between palm-center and the user's head position, so the arc always faces the user as the hand rotates.
  • Slots: up to 8, evenly distributed; 6 is the default (menu length).
  • Slot collider: a 2.5 cm sphere; selection fires when the other hand's index-fingertip enters the sphere and the other hand is in a "pointing" pose (fingers 2-5 curled > 60°).
  • Dismissal: palm rotates away from the user by more than 60°, or the user explicitly touches a "close" slot at the arc endpoint.

docs.title: What this ADR is NOT committing to
docs.text:
• The AR passthrough plumbing (still in issue #9).
  • The hand-tracking driver choice (Meta XR SDK vs. OpenXR direct).
  • The 2D fallback render — already in ARSemicirclePanel.kt.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Flat version renders inside the nostalgic home surface as a design preview.
  • World-space version is the work of issue #9 and ADR 0010 (TBD, driver choice).
  • Tests can live against the pure geometry calculation (take palm + head pose, return 8 slot world positions) without needing a headset.

docs.title: Alternatives rejected
docs.text:
• 270° ring: looked "cooler" but rejected because sideways slots require head rotation to see.
  • Icon-grid in air: fine for 2D but doesn't match the "hand as menu" intent of the design brief.

docs.title: ADR 0009 — Root gating: detect, don't elevate
docs.text: Status: Accepted · 2026-11-07

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
Several QuestClassic features (strip-Meta, firmware dump, boot-animation swap, dev-super-mode, home-menu swapper) are only possible on a device where root has been enabled by some external means — a userdebug/eng build, a signed vendor image, or a Magisk install the user performed after unlocking an older firmware's bootloader.

We had to decide:

  1. Ship the exploit ourselves. Build a root-exploit chain into the APK so any installer gets root for free. Rejected: see below.
  2. Refuse to show the feature at all unless rooted. Hide the UI. Rejected: users deserve to see what's possible and why it's gated.
  3. Show the UI; detect root at runtime; only execute the privileged action on rooted devices, with a verbose explanation on stock. ✅ Accepted.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
Every privileged panel is built with:

  • A RootDetector runtime probe that returns a confidence rating from NONE to HIGH.
  • A RootGateCard composable that explains, in plain terms:
  • Whether root was detected (and which signals fired).
  • What this panel would do if root were available.
  • What the honest adb/shell commands look like.
  • The destructive action is only enabled when RootStatus.isRooted == true.
  • On a stock device the panel is a dry-run. You can read the plan, copy the shell commands, audit them, and run them manually via ADB on your own authority.

docs.title: Why not ship the exploit
docs.text:
1. Physical impossibility for the keys that matter. Signing/encryption keys live in Qualcomm silicon fuses + QSEE TrustZone. No userspace exploit retrieves them, because the hardware fuse-rooted keybox is designed specifically against this.
  2. Legal risk. Distributing a rooting tool targeting a consumer device with signed boot likely violates DMCA 1201 anti-circumvention. The security-research exemption doesn't cover tools built primarily to circumvent.
  3. Downstream harm. A rooting tool on GitHub targets anyone's Quest, not just the installer's. Resold devices, kids' devices, stolen devices — the tool doesn't know.
  4. Brittleness. Public Quest-2 root chains have historically relied on specific old-firmware vulns that Meta patched. Shipping one in-app would mean the app bricks itself on any updated device.

docs.title: Why not hide the UI
docs.text:
1. Transparency. Users want to know what's possible on their device even if they can't act today.
  2. Documentation value. The dry-run panels are living documentation of what an advanced user could do with root + ADB.
  3. Education. A visible "this requires root, here's why, here's the exact adb you'd run" is more useful to the ecosystem than a hidden feature.

docs.title: Consequences
docs.text:
• Every root-gated panel in QuestClassic carries RootGateCard prominently.
  • The panels' plans (shell commands) are visible to the user; nothing is hidden.
  • On a rooted device, actions run; on a stock device, nothing writes.
  • Users on stock devices who want more are directed to responsible sources (XDA, Magisk forums) rather than the app itself.

docs.title: Related ADRs
docs.text:
• 0004 · No telemetry — the privileges we DO have we don't abuse.
  • 0005 · GitHub Releases as update channel — no Meta cloud involved.

docs.title: Future revisits
docs.text: • If a public, non-weaponizable root unlock becomes available for Quest 2 and the ecosystem has moved on (devices long-EOL), we could revisit linking to external root tooling from the app. We will not bundle it.

docs.title: Compose UI — what we use and what we don't
docs.text: Jetpack Compose is the only UI toolkit in the project. No XML layouts, no Fragments beyond what Compose needs under the hood, no view binding, no databinding. Rationale in ADR 0002.

docs.title: What we use
docs.text:
• setContent { } in MainActivity as the single entry point to the UI.
  • Material3 (androidx.compose.material3) for Button, OutlinedTextField, Text, MaterialTheme.
  • Material icons extended (androidx.compose.material.icons.outlined.*) for tile icons.
  • Compose Foundation for layout + gestures: Box, Row, Column, LazyColumn, LazyVerticalGrid, Modifier.clickable, etc.
  • Compose Runtime state: remember, mutableStateOf, mutableIntStateOf, mutableStateListOf, LaunchedEffect, rememberCoroutineScope, derivedStateOf where relevant.
  • Activity Compose for rememberLauncherForActivityResult.
  • Navigation — we do it ourselves with a HomeScreen enum + when dispatch (NostalgicHomeScreen.kt). No Navigation Compose for v0.1.0; we'll consider it when the panel count passes ~15.

docs.title: What we don't use
docs.text:
• XML layouts. Zero layout files under res/layout.
  • View Binding / Data Binding. Not enabled.
  • Fragments. Zero direct usage; Compose uses them internally under ComponentActivity but we never write one.
  • Compose Preview @Preview on most components — the whole app runs on the headset, not on previews. We'd add previews if we started hitting Studio for UI iteration.
  • Fancy Compose libraries: no Accompanist (deprecated anyway), no Coil (no images beyond app icons via BitmapDrawable), no Compose Charts.

docs.title: Our reusable Composables
docs.text:
All in ui/nostalgic/NostalgicComponents.kt:

  • GlassPanel(modifier, onClick?, accent) { content } — the primary surface card with the dark navy gradient and teal accent border. Every panel uses it.
  • ChipLabel(text, color) — small pill-shaped status chip.
  • StatRow(label, value, ok) — key/value row with a green/red indicator dot.
  • PanelHeader(title, subtitle, chip?) — the "label + title + optional chip" masthead at the top of each panel.
  • TileButton(icon, title, description, onClick) — the 2×N home-grid tile.

In ui/panels/LauncherPanel.kt:

  • PanelClose(title, subtitle, onClose) — close affordance at the top of every panel. (Lives in LauncherPanel.kt because that's the first panel that needed it; refactoring out into NostalgicComponents is tracked informally.)

docs.title: Composable naming
docs.text:
• Top-level panels are *Panel.
  • Private helpers inside a panel are lowercase local functions or @Composable named AppTile, AIConfigForm, AIField, ClockWidget, etc.
  • Everything in ui.nostalgic is public to the module so panels can reuse.

docs.title: State management
docs.text:
• Local UI state (remember { mutableStateOf(…) }) lives in the Composable that owns it.
  • Repository-backed state flows in through AppContainer (which is in turn remembered at the MainActivity level, passed down as a param).
  • No ViewModels anywhere in v0.1.0. rememberCoroutineScope + LaunchedEffect cover everything. We'll add viewModel() when a panel's state has to survive config changes (e.g. after real AR integration).

docs.title: Theming
docs.text:
See architecture/theming.md. Short version:

  • Force dark scheme always — this is a VR shell app; no light mode makes sense inside a headset.
  • Palette lives in ui/theme/Theme.kt as QCColors.
  • Typography uses only system fonts (FontFamily.SansSerif / Monospace) — no font downloads, no Google Fonts call at runtime.

docs.title: Known rough edges
docs.text:
• NetworkPingWidget in BuildToolsPanel.kt uses a hand-rolled CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.IO).launch — should move to rememberCoroutineScope for proper cancellation on nav-away. Tracked as a cleanup PR candidate.
  • AIAssistantPanel's input field doesn't show a send-on-enter — Quest keyboards don't send IME actions reliably and we haven't wired an alternative. Logging ticket worth filing.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Coroutines & threading
docs.text: How work actually runs in this app.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. All Composables run on main. Nothing blocking in a Composable body.
  2. All I/O (disk, network, crypto) runs on Dispatchers.IO via explicit withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { … }.
  3. UI effects (fire-and-forget on user action) use rememberCoroutineScope. That scope is cancelled when the Composable leaves composition, so no leaks.
  4. Fire-and-forget without a scope is a bug. The one exception right now is NetworkPingWidget, which we noted as a cleanup target.
  5. No GlobalScope. Ever.

docs.title: Background load on panel open
docs.text:
var apps by remember { mutableStateOf<List<InstalledApp>>(emptyList()) }
LaunchedEffect(Unit) { apps = container.appList.load() }

LaunchedEffect(Unit) runs once when the Composable enters composition; if the user navigates away before it finishes, Compose cancels it.

docs.title: User-triggered async work
docs.text:
val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
Button(onClick = {
    scope.launch {
        running = true
        results = container.diagnostics.runAll()
        container.diagnostics.buzzFailures(results)
        running = false
    }
})

rememberCoroutineScope() gives you a CoroutineScope tied to the Composable. Launches on it get cancelled on nav-away.

docs.title: Repository-level background work
docs.text:
Repositories use withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { … } internally; callers (Composables) stay on main:

suspend fun load(): List<InstalledApp> = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    // heavy PackageManager queries here
}

docs.title: Parallel fan-out
docs.text:
For the Meta Hosts Audit we probe 24 hosts in parallel:

val results = MetaHostsAudit.all.map { host ->
    async { MetaHostsAudit.probe(host) }
}.awaitAll()

async + awaitAll on the current scope. No manual thread pool.

docs.title: Why not Flow?
docs.text: For the current panel set, remember { mutableStateOf(…) } + one-shot LaunchedEffect covers every use case cleanly. StateFlow + collectAsState is strictly more verbose for the same outcome here. When we have long-lived subscriptions (a notification stream, continuous diagnostics, real OpenXR frame data) we'll adopt Flow there and keep plain State elsewhere.

docs.title: Why not a ViewModel per panel?
docs.text:
ViewModels survive configuration changes (rotation, dark-mode flip, keyboard open). On a Quest 2:

  • No rotation changes — the headset's primary-display orientation is baked in.
  • No dark-mode toggling — we force dark scheme.
  • No system keyboard typically — VR apps bring their own.

So a Composable's rememberSaveable lifetime matches a ViewModel's for our panels. Adding ViewModels would be extra ceremony with no behavior difference. We'll adopt them when state has to outlive a Composable (e.g. real AR mode's immersive frame pipeline).

docs.title: Cancellation safety
docs.text:
A test worth running yourself after adding a long-running coroutine: mid-work, tap the panel's Close button. If anything keeps running past that, you have a scope leak. The current codebase has one known leak (the ping widget); everything else cleans up correctly.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: DI container
docs.text: One hand-wired class. See ADR 0003 for the full reasoning.

docs.title: The container
docs.text:
class AppContainer(private val app: Context) {
    val http: OkHttpClient = OkHttpClient.Builder()
        .connectTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .readTimeout(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .build()

    val appList: AppListRepository = AppListRepository(app)
    val haptics: ControllerHaptics = ControllerHaptics(app)
    val diagnostics: DiagnosticsEngine = DiagnosticsEngine(app, haptics)
    val introspection: DeviceIntrospection = DeviceIntrospection(app)
    val updater: SelfUpdater = SelfUpdater(app, http)
    val ai: AIRepository = AIRepository(app, http)
    val payloadVerifier: PayloadVerifier = PayloadVerifier(app)
    val systemProbe: SystemPropertyProbe = SystemPropertyProbe()
}

That's the whole container. Created once in QuestClassicApplication.onCreate(); passed as a val container: AppContainer into setContent → NostalgicHomeScreen(container) → every panel.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. Nothing outside the container constructs a repository. If you need one, add a val here.
  2. Nothing stashes a Context long-term — the container holds Application scope (safe) and passes it down; panels use LocalContext.current when they need the current Context.
  3. No circular deps. The declaration order in AppContainer is the dependency order; if a repo depends on another, the dependency is declared earlier. Right now the only intra-container dep is DiagnosticsEngine(app, haptics).
  4. No lazy init unless you need to defer a real cost. Everything above is cheap to construct.

docs.title: Why not Hilt / Dagger / Koin / Anvil?
docs.text:
• Hilt / Dagger: KAPT or KSP, annotation processing, several hundred ms of extra build time, debuggable only through generated code. Worth it on multi-module 50+-screen apps; wildly over-engineered at 10 panels.
  • Koin: lightweight-ish but runtime graph construction, error-at-runtime (missing binding → crash at first read), DSL lock-in.
  • Anvil: the Dagger-with-Compose-friendly variant; same arguments as Dagger.
  • Hand-wired: every dependency is a plain Kotlin val, compile-time-verified, 0 ms of annotation processing, you read the container and you know what exists.

If this app ever grows to 15+ panels or starts needing per-user scopes, we'll revisit. Until then: one class.

docs.title: Adding a new dependency
docs.text:
1. Open core/AppContainer.kt.
  2. Add one line: val mything: MyThing = MyThing(app, http) (or whatever args it needs).
  3. Done. Any panel that takes a container: AppContainer can now use container.mything.

If your new thing needs another new thing, declare that one first in the container. The lint rule is just: later lines can refer to earlier vals.

docs.title: Request flow — the longest path
docs.text:
User taps Signature Verifier → Pick OTA:

LauncherPanel ▸ sys file-picker ▸ ActivityResultContracts.OpenDocument
                      ↓ user picks .zip
PayloadVerifier.verify(uri)
  on Dispatchers.IO
  ▸ ContentResolver.openInputStream
    ▸ ZipInputStream → extract payload.bin + otacert.pem
  ▸ RandomAccessFile(payload.bin, "r")
    ▸ read CrAU header → parse version / manifest_size / meta_sig_size
    ▸ SHA-256 pass 1 (header + manifest)
    ▸ parse Signatures protobuf → RSA sig bytes
    ▸ Signature.getInstance("NONEwithRSA") → verify
    ▸ parse manifest → find signatures_offset / _size
    ▸ SHA-256 pass 2 (header + manifest + data_blobs section)
    ▸ parse 2nd Signatures protobuf → verify
  → Report(digests, valid/invalid per sig, cert subject/issuer/fingerprint)
Panel redraws with the glass cards

Where it touches Android: ContentResolver + ZipInputStream + RandomAccessFile. Where it touches Java crypto: MessageDigest, Signature, CertificateFactory. Where it touches our code: three Kotlin files. That's it.

docs.text:

  • No app-level singletons aside from AppContainer itself.

docs.title: On-device storage
docs.text: Where we put things and why.

docs.title: DataStore (Preferences)
docs.text:
One file:

/data/data/io.github.questclassic.app/datastore/ai_config.preferences_pb

Keys:

Key Type Purpose name String Assistant name backend String Backend ID (claude / openai / ollama) model String Optional model override api_key String Sensitive. The AI provider's API key or Ollama base URL. prompt String System prompt

Backed by androidx.datastore.preferences.preferencesDataStore("ai_config") — same file format as SharedPreferences but with coroutine-safe writes and no cross-process concerns.

docs.title: Why DataStore and not SharedPreferences
docs.text: SharedPreferences has well-known bugs on config change + commit-vs-apply races. DataStore is the modern replacement. Overhead is zero; API is cleaner.

docs.title: Why not encrypted storage
docs.text:
• The DataStore file is already in app-private storage (world-unreadable).
  • On a rooted headset, encryption-at-rest with a user-derived key would offer marginal protection against someone who already has root.
  • Android Keystore-backed encryption is possible (Jetpack Security crypto) and has a cost we didn't want to pay in v0.1.0. security/known-limits.md notes this.

docs.title: Excluded from Android cloud backup
docs.text:
res/xml/data_extraction_rules.xml lists this file as excluded from both cloud backup and device-transfer:

<cloud-backup>
    <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="ai_config.preferences_pb" />
</cloud-backup>
<device-transfer>
    <exclude domain="sharedpref" path="ai_config.preferences_pb" />
</device-transfer>

So your API key never flows to Google Drive (even though it's unlikely to on a Quest; the Quest doesn't integrate with Android auto-backup the way a phone does).

docs.title: Cache dir
docs.text:
context.cacheDir — used for:

  • Downloaded APK during self-update → cacheDir/questclassic-update.apk. Replaced on each update; Android purges it under memory pressure, which is fine.
  • Temp payload.bin extraction during signature verification (streamed from the picked .zip into a temp file, then deleted when verification returns). We use File.deleteOnExit() + an explicit finally { file.delete() }.

The cache dir is exposed to the FileProvider via res/xml/file_provider_paths.xml:

<cache-path name="updates" path="." />

Which means the system's package installer can read questclassic-update.apk through a content:// URI without us needing WRITE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE.

docs.title: Everything else is ephemeral
docs.text:
• Diagnostics results: lifetime = one panel visit.
  • AI chat history: in-memory SnapshotStateList. Cleared on Composable nav-away. Intentional — the panel is for quick ad-hoc chats, not sessions.
  • Quick note widget: in-memory mutableStateOf(""). Cleared on Composable nav-away.
  • Meta Hosts Audit results: in-memory SnapshotStateList. Re-runs on panel open.

docs.title: Why so little persisted
docs.text:
v0.1.0 is small enough that most "state" is cheap to recompute. We'll add DataStore-backed persistence to the Quick Note widget and to Build Tools widget selection as issues get picked up (see docs/widget_sdk.md).

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Theming & the nostalgic look
docs.text: The retro-Oculus aesthetic in one page: palette, typography, components.

docs.title: Palette (QCColors)
docs.text:
Name Hex Role Space #07122A App background, deep Deep #0E1E3F Background gradient low, panel base Panel #13274F Glass panel top-color Edge #1E3666 Borders, inactive buttons, dividers Teal #34E5E7 Primary accent — VR tiles, active buttons, links Amber #FFB347 Secondary accent — 2D tiles, warnings, chips Soft #D7E2FF Foreground text Dim #7F91B9 Secondary / label text Warn #FF6E6E Failure state OK #66E0A3 Pass state

The Space→Deep gradient is the signature background. Panels sit on a Panel→Deep sub-gradient inside a Teal 35%-alpha border. That border tint flips to Amber or Warn or OK depending on the panel's state.

docs.title: Why this palette
docs.text:
• Oculus Rift / early Gear VR era shells used deep navy with teal highlights. We're invoking that.
  • High contrast against the Quest OLED-adjacent panels — pure black glows, pure white burns in VR; we offset.
  • Teal + amber reads as "retro-tech" rather than "modern Quest" (which leans white + blue).
  • Warn / OK stay away from brand accents so they don't get confused with just "active."

Rationale: VR headsets are worn eyes-first; a bright white UI inside a dark room kills your night vision and blooms on OLED. Dark is the right default; we don't offer light.

docs.title: Suggested first-day sequence to earn 4 badges
docs.text:
1. Push the initial repo → auto release of v0.1.0 tag → Pull Shark #1 (via main-branch commits counted as implicit PRs). (Note: Pull Shark counts merged PRs, so…)
  2. Open PR #1: "fix typo in README". Merge without review → YOLO.

  4. Any CI commit already carries Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 4.7 <noreply@anthropic.com> if generated via this collaboration → Pair Extraordinaire.
  5. Merge the Free-memory widget PR → Pull Shark (2 PRs).

docs.title: What we don't do
docs.text:
• Create fake accounts or coordinate star-trading rings. GitHub detects and penalizes both.
  • Spam issues/PRs for the sake of counting. Each PR in this repo does real work (a widget, a buzz pattern, a backend).
  • Automate reactions — Heart on Your Sleeve is nice but it's not something the repo structure should chase at the expense of readability.

docs.title: Coding standards
docs.text: Short because Kotlin + Compose give us most of this for free.

docs.title: Kotlin
docs.text:
• kotlin.code.style=official is in gradle.properties. 4-space indent. Tabs are banned.
  • Max line length: ~120. Nobody's rejecting a PR for 125; nobody's writing 200-column lines either.
  • val by default; var when you mean "this changes."
  • Prefer expression body for short functions: 
    fun double(x: Int): Int = x * 2
  • Null safety: use ?., ?:, let, runCatching. Avoid !! unless the invariant is literally impossible to violate.
  • Return Result<T> from suspending functions that can fail in expected ways (network, parse, permission).
  • One class per file where the class has substance; multiple short enums/data-classes per file is fine.

docs.title: Compose
docs.text:
• Composable names: PascalCase.
  • Composables take modifier: Modifier = Modifier as the FIRST modifier param, not last.
  • State lives in the Composable that owns it unless lifting is justified.
  • Stateless Composables are preferred — they take data in, call back out.
  • Private Composables (file-scoped helpers) are private fun, not internal.
  • Never block the main thread. If something might: Dispatchers.IO via withContext.
  • Preview functions optional; the headset is the real preview.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text:
• Repositories end in Repository (AppListRepository, AIRepository).
  • Engines end in Engine (DiagnosticsEngine).
  • Panels end in Panel (LauncherPanel, AIAssistantPanel).
  • Activities end in Activity.
  • Interfaces have no I prefix. We're Kotlin, not AIDL.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• New deps go through security/dependencies.md' review bar.
  • Pin versions in gradle/libs.versions.toml. No floating versions.
  • No transitive forcing without a reason in the PR.

docs.title: Comments
docs.text:
Default to writing none. Add a comment only when the "why" is non-obvious. See the project-wide guidance in CONTRIBUTING.md.

Prefer:

// AOSP ships this field in little-endian on A/B v2+; big-endian on legacy. We're A/B-only.
val version = struct.unpack("<Q", header)

Not:

// Parse the version
val version = struct.unpack("<Q", header)

docs.title: Formatting
docs.text:
Run Android Studio's "Reformat Code" on changed files. Don't reformat files you're not touching. The project doesn't have ktlint or detekt wired up yet; low on the priority list but a good first PR candidate.

• Source: everything under docs/ + the root README.md, with the nav in mkdocs.yml.
  • Theme: mkdocs-material 9.5.44 (pinned in .github/workflows/docs.yml).
  • Trigger: push to main that touches docs/, README.md, mkdocs.yml, or the workflow itself.
  • Workflow: .github/workflows/docs.yml — two jobs, build then deploy.
  • Deploy target: GitHub Pages, env github-pages.

docs.title: First-time repo setup
docs.text:
1. Repo → Settings → Pages → Source → "GitHub Actions".
  2. That's it — the next push to main under docs/ triggers a build and deploy.

docs.title: Local preview
docs.text:
pip install mkdocs-material==9.5.44
make serve-docs
# open http://127.0.0.1:8000

Or mkdocs serve directly.

docs.title: Strict mode
docs.text:
The workflow builds with --strict, so any:

  • broken internal link,
  • missing nav entry,
  • Markdown that produces a warning

fails the build. That's deliberate; the docs are supposed to stay internally consistent.

docs.title: Adding a new page
docs.text:
1. Write the .md file somewhere under docs/.
  2. Add it to mkdocs.yml's nav: tree at the right spot.
  3. Open a PR; CI will verify the link graph and the deploy preview.

docs.title: Known pain points
docs.text:
• Changing mkdocs.yml's theme palette breaks Pages cache for ~2 min. Hard-refresh once if colors look stale.
  • Pages deploy needs the repo to have Pages enabled. The first-time setup step above is manual (GitHub won't let the workflow enable it for you).

docs.title: Getting started as a contributor
docs.text: Clone, build, run, land a PR — in 15 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• JDK 17 (any distribution; Temurin is fine).
  • Android SDK (easiest via Android Studio — install once, accept licenses).
  • adb on your PATH.
  • A Quest 2+ with Developer Mode enabled OR an AOSP Cuttlefish instance OR any Android 10+ device/emulator.

docs.title: Build + run
docs.text:
git clone https://github.com/A-Hackers-Guide/QuestClassic.git
cd QuestClassic
./gradlew :app:assembleDebug
adb install app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk

Gradle fetches deps on first build (~5 min). Subsequent builds are seconds.

docs.title: Add an AI backend
docs.text:
1. cp app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ai/OpenAIBackend.kt \ app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ai/GeminiBackend.kt
  2. Edit: change id, displayName, endpoint, request shape per Google Gemini's API docs.
  3. Register in AIRepository.backends.
  4. Build. Done.

Walkthrough details in the AI Companion user guide.

docs.title: Add a diagnostic buzz pattern
docs.text:
1. Open app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/core/ControllerHaptics.kt.
  2. Add a constant to BuzzPattern.Companion: 
    val MY_FAULT = BuzzPattern("-.-.-", "my fault description")
  3. Add a row to docs/reference/buzz-patterns.md.
  4. Wire it up to the detection in core/DiagnosticsEngine.kt.

docs.title: Add a Build Tools widget
docs.text:
1. Open app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ui/panels/BuildToolsPanel.kt.
  2. Add an entry to Widget: 
    MY_WIDGET("My widget", @Composable { c -> MyWidget(c) }),
  3. Write @Composable private fun MyWidget(container: AppContainer) { ... } in the same file.
  4. Update the widget row in the Build Tools user guide.

docs.title: Add a whole new panel
docs.text:
1. Create app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ui/panels/MyPanel.kt:
@Composable
fun MyPanel(container: AppContainer, onClose: () -> Unit) {
    Column(Modifier.fillMaxSize()) {
        PanelClose(title = "My panel", subtitle = "…", onClose = onClose)
        Spacer(Modifier.height(16.dp))
        GlassPanel(modifier = Modifier.fillMaxWidth()) {
            Text("Hello from my panel", color = QCColors.Soft)
        }
    }
}
  1. In NostalgicHomeScreen.kt:
  2. Add MY to the HomeScreen enum.
  3. Add the when branch dispatching to MyPanel.

  4. Add a HomeTile entry.

  5. Add a docs/user-guide/my-panel.md and link it from docs/README.md.

  6. PR.

docs.title: PR process
docs.text: See contributing/pr-process.md.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text:
See contributing/testing.md. Short version: there's no formal test suite yet; the first unit tests (for PayloadVerifier) are issue #12.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Good first issues
docs.text: Pick one; comment "I'll take this"; open a PR.

docs.title: Live right now
docs.text:
• #6 — Add a new AI backend (Gemini / Mistral / Groq) — one new file + one line in AIRepository. Ship-rateable in an evening.
  • #7 — Add a new diagnostic buzz pattern — one BuzzPattern constant + table row + wire-up. Scope is tiny.
  • #8 — Add a new Build Tools widget — any widget from the "to land" list in the Build Tools user guide. Scope is tiny.

docs.title: What makes a good first issue
docs.text:
• Scoped to a few files.
  • Visible outcome — the user sees something change.
  • Doesn't require Quest hardware to validate (AOSP Cuttlefish or any Android device works).
  • No undocumented dependency on another incomplete feature.

docs.title: Not a good first issue
docs.text:
• OpenXR integration (#9). Big. Load-bearing. Save for someone with Quest-dev experience.
  • Signing keystore setup (#11) — infrastructure-level, needs access to the repo's secrets.

docs.title: How to find more
docs.text:
Filter the issue list by label good first issue:

https://github.com/A-Hackers-Guide/QuestClassic/issues?q=is%3Aopen+label%3A%22good+first+issue%22

If the list is empty, that's a sign you should pick a roadmap bullet and split off a focused issue.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: PR process
docs.text: Fork, branch, commit, push, open PR, address review, merge.

docs.title: Branch names
docs.text: feat/thing-you're-adding, fix/thing-you're-fixing, docs/..., chore/..., refactor/.... Not patch-1 or main on your fork.

docs.title: Commit messages
docs.text:
Imperative mood ("feat: add widget" not "feat: added widget"). Optional scope. Description sometimes helpful; the diff usually says what.

feat(ai): add Gemini backend

Implements AIBackend against the Gemini v1beta API. User supplies
their own Google AI Studio key in the Configure form.

Signed-off / co-authored-by trailers welcome.

docs.title: Opening the PR
docs.text:
Title = one-line summary (what the changelog line would say).

Body = the four-section standard:

  • What — plain English.
  • Why — the motivation / the issue it closes.
  • How — the approach, if non-obvious.
  • Test plan — what you did to verify.

If the PR touches a user-facing panel, include a short description of the before/after. Screenshots welcome.

docs.title: Review
docs.text:
• Solo maintainers right now, so "approved" is often "merged by author after green CI."
  • CI must be green (both Build and, if the PR touches shipped behavior, any test that lands in issue #12).
  • If there are no reviewers, a 24-hour hold is a reasonable self-imposed delay to catch obvious issues.

docs.title: Merging
docs.text:
• Squash merge is the default. One PR = one commit on main.
  • Don't merge on a red CI unless the breakage is unrelated and tracked.
  • Delete the branch after merge.

docs.title: After merging
docs.text:
• Any issue referenced by Closes #N auto-closes.
  • Release notes auto-generate from merged PR titles when we next tag v*.

docs.title: If you can't finish a PR
docs.text:
• Mark it a Draft (gh pr ready -u).
  • Add a note. Someone may pick it up; no pressure.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Release process
docs.text: How we cut a version. Takes about 5 minutes.

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• You're on main, up-to-date, clean.
  • CI on main's latest commit is green.
  • CHANGELOG.md has a "Unreleased" section with the changes you're about to ship.

docs.title: 1. Decide the version
docs.text:
Semver-adjacent:

  • MAJOR (v1.0.0) — breaking change the user has to deal with (keystore change, removed feature, etc.).
  • MINOR (v0.2.0) — new features, no breaking changes.
  • PATCH (v0.1.1) — bug fixes only.

Pre-release: v0.2.0-rc.1. The CI's prerelease: contains(ref_name, '-') marks these correctly.

docs.title: 2. Promote Unreleased → new version in CHANGELOG
docs.text:
## [0.2.0] - 2026-12-01
### Added
- Gemini AI backend (#17)
- Free memory widget (#8)
...

Commit:

git commit -am "chore: release v0.2.0"
git push origin main

docs.title: 3. Tag
docs.text:
git tag v0.2.0 -m "QuestClassic v0.2.0"
git push origin v0.2.0

docs.title: 4. Watch CI
docs.text:
release.yml fires on tag push. It:

  1. Checks out the tagged commit.
  2. seds the self-updater to point at the right repo.
  3. Decodes the signing keystore (if QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_B64 secret is set).
  4. Runs ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease.
  5. Creates a GitHub Release with auto-generated notes.
  6. Attaches app/build/outputs/apk/release/*.apk.

Typical runtime: 2-3 minutes.

docs.title: 5. Verify
docs.text:
• Open the release on GitHub, confirm the APK is attached.
  • Download it, SHA-256 it, note the fingerprint.
  • Install on your headset (adb install -r -d app-release.apk).
  • Open the Updates panel and verify "You're on the latest."

docs.title: 6. Announce
docs.text:
• Pin the release note in the project Discussions, if you've enabled them.
  • Update any downstream docs that reference a version.

docs.title: If something's wrong
docs.text:
• CI failed: fix on main, delete the bad tag locally and remotely, re-tag: 
    git tag -d v0.2.0
git push origin :refs/tags/v0.2.0
gh release delete v0.2.0 --yes
# fix, commit, push
git tag v0.2.0 && git push origin v0.2.0
  • APK attached but broken: don't try to patch in place. Cut v0.2.1.

docs.title: When to cut a prerelease
docs.text:
• You want to test the release pipeline itself (e.g. after changing release.yml).
  • You're about to ship a big feature and want testers first.
  • Tag it v0.2.0-rc.1; the CI marks it prerelease: true.

The Updates panel ignores prereleases by default — if a - appears in the tag, isNewer still flags it but the release itself is marked prerelease on GitHub, which by convention consumers filter out.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Testing
docs.text: v0.1.0 has no formal test suite. First tests land for PayloadVerifier (see issue #12).

docs.title: What we test today
docs.text:
• Manual on-device testing. Every PR gets sideloaded and the touched panel exercised.
  • CI compiles. ./gradlew :app:assembleDebug (build.yml) + :app:assembleRelease (release.yml) on every push and PR.
  • Signature Verifier is cross-checked against tools/verify_payload.py — if the Kotlin port and the Python reference ever disagree, that's a bug.

docs.title: What to test if you add a feature
docs.text:
• New panel: open, close, open again (state reset). Rotate (shouldn't apply on Quest; still try on Cuttlefish). Kill the app, reopen.
  • New AI backend: correct backend selected in the picker. Invalid API key returns a clean error message (not a crash). Valid key + minimal prompt returns a reply.
  • New diagnostic: fire the condition (unplug Wi-Fi, fill storage, etc.) and verify the pattern fires on the controllers.
  • New widget: toggle on + off. Verify it stops ticking when off.
  • Anything crypto / parser (PayloadVerifier, pbdump, etc.): add fuzz-style tests. Even quick ones.

docs.title: Running existing tests (none yet)
docs.text:
./gradlew :app:testDebugUnitTest

Returns success because nothing's there. First PR to add a test should also:

  • Enable testImplementation(libs.junit.jupiter) or kotlin.test in app/build.gradle.kts.
  • Create app/src/test/kotlin/....
  • Run the test locally once.
  • Make sure CI picks it up (should Just Work with testDebugUnitTest).

docs.title: Instrumented tests
docs.text:
Not v0.1.0. Would need Android Test Orchestrator + emulator hosts in CI. Tracked loosely for after v0.2.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Toolchain uplift plan (tracking #28)
docs.text: Dependabot opened five Gradle-dep PRs that all failed CI because they're major-version jumps that depend on a newer JVM, Gradle, Kotlin, or Android SDK. Merging them piecemeal would thrash the build. This doc is the coordinated uplift plan we'll execute in one PR before Dependabot's next sweep.

docs.title: Target baseline
docs.text: Thing Current Target Why JDK 17 21 (LTS) AGP 9.x hard-requires 21. Gradle wrapper 8.10.2 9.0.0+ AGP 9.x requires Gradle 9. Kotlin 2.0.21 2.1.0+ Needed by compose-bom 2026.09 and the kotlinx-serialization 1.12 release train. AGP (com.android.application) 8.6.1 9.5.1 Current latest; brings the modern lint rules + non-transitive R classes default. compileSdk 35 36 Needed by datastore-preferences 1.3 and navigation-compose 2.10. targetSdk 35 36 Match compileSdk. minSdk 29 29 Unchanged — see ADR 0007; dropping Quest 2 users is a non-goal. JUnit 4.13.2 4.13.2 Unchanged; our tests are JVM-only.

docs.title: The piecemeal Dependabot PRs waiting on this
docs.text:
PR Bump Blocker #18 (closed) kotlinx-serialization 1.7.3 → 1.12.0 Kotlin 2.1+ #20 (closed) datastore-preferences 1.1.1 → 1.3.0 compileSdk 36 #21 (closed) navigation-compose 2.8.4 → 2.10.2 compileSdk 36 #22 (closed) compose-bom 2024.10.01 → 2026.09.00 Kotlin 2.1+ #23 (closed) AGP 8.6.1 → 9.5.1 JDK 21, Gradle 9

All five were closed with a pointer to #28. Dependabot re-proposes the same bumps on its next weekly cycle, which gives us one week to land the uplift before they pile up again.

docs.title: Execution order
docs.text:
1. CI: bump JDK 17 → 21 in both build.yml and release.yml. One commit. Verify CI still passes.
  2. Gradle wrapper: ./gradlew wrapper --gradle-version 9.0.0 --distribution-type bin and commit gradle/wrapper/*. CI run.
  3. Kotlin 2.0.21 → 2.1.0 in libs.versions.toml under kotlin ref. Run ./gradlew :app:compileDebugKotlin locally; may surface deprecations.
  4. AGP 8.6.1 → 9.5.1 in libs.versions.toml under agp. Expect AGP 9 to tighten several lint rules; address them in the same PR.
  5. compileSdk + targetSdk 35 → 36 in app/build.gradle.kts. One file.
  6. The 4 held-back deps (compose-bom, navigation-compose, datastore-preferences, kotlinx-serialization) — bump each ref in libs.versions.toml.
  7. Lint pass — run ./gradlew :app:lintDebug and fix anything new.

All 7 steps in one PR titled chore: toolchain uplift (JDK 21, Gradle 9, Kotlin 2.1, AGP 9.5, compileSdk 36).

docs.title: Risks
docs.text:
• AGP 9's namespace enforcement. If any legacy R class path exists it will break. We don't have any, but AGP 9 may still surface strict warnings.
  • Compose BOM 2026.09. New Compose adds a lot of API deprecations around Modifier.foundation and Text overloads. Expect 10-20 small call-site changes.
  • Kotlin 2.1 K2 fallout. The new K2 compiler frontend is default; some of our edgier type inference calls may need explicit types.
  • Gradle 9's configuration cache. AGP 9 enables it by default; a task that doesn't support it will be loud.

docs.title: Fallback
docs.text: If the uplift PR takes more than ~3 hours of hand-holding, revert the AGP bump (back to 8.7.x which is still 2024-current) and keep JDK 21 + Kotlin 2.1 + compileSdk 36 as the baseline. That still unblocks 3 of the 5 Dependabot PRs.

docs.title: Who's assigned
docs.text: Open — pick up #28 if you want to drive it.

docs.title: Enable Developer Mode on your Meta account
docs.text: Meta gates sideloading behind a "Developer Mode" flag. It's a one-time flip on your account, free, and doesn't void your warranty, revoke your subscription, or anything else theatrical.

docs.title: What you'll do
docs.text: Register (or join) a developer organization on Meta's dashboard, flip the toggle on your account, then enable it on the headset itself from the Meta mobile app.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. On a PC or phone browser, open developer.meta.com/manage and sign in with the same Meta account you use on the headset.
  2. If prompted, create a new organization. Pick any name — it's just an internal ID — and accept the developer terms.
  3. Open the Meta Horizon app (used to be "Oculus app") on your phone. The phone needs to be paired with the headset already.
  4. Tap Menu → Devices → (your headset) → Headset Settings → Developer Mode.
  5. Flip it on.

docs.title: Verify
docs.text: Put the headset on. Go to Settings → System → Developer. You should see the developer menu — if you don't, Meta hasn't rolled the flag through yet. Give it a few minutes, maybe a reboot of the headset, then check again.

docs.title: What this changes on your account
docs.text:
• You can install APKs over ADB (what we use here).
  • You can run adb logcat and read your own device's logs.
  • You get access to a couple of "Developer" toggles in the headset settings (passthrough debugging, forced permissions dialogs, etc.).

docs.title: What this doesn't change
docs.text:
• No bootloader unlock, no root, no AVB bypass.
  • No change to purchases, subscriptions, warranty, or support eligibility.
  • No visible sign to Meta's Store that you're a developer — you buy games the same way.

docs.title: Opting back out
docs.text:
Turn it off in the same phone-app menu. Headset-side developer menu disappears a reboot later.

Last reviewed against Meta Horizon mobile app v242 and the developer.meta.com dashboard, Nov 2026. Meta renames things — if the exact menu paths drift, the concept hasn't moved.

docs.title: First launch
docs.text: What happens the first time you open QuestClassic on the headset, and what you can do in the next 10 minutes.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
A dark navy background with a big "SHELF" masthead and a 2×4 grid of tiles:

Tile What it opens Launcher Every app on the headset in a retro grid Diagnostics Runs 6 self-tests and buzzes the controllers on any fail AI Companion Setup form the first time, chat UI after Build Tools Programmable HUD Updates Checks GitHub for a newer QuestClassic About / System Device details, the experimental AR Home launcher Signature Verifier Pick an OTA .zip, verify its Meta signatures System Internals Live view of HorizonOS quirks Meta Hosts Audit Resolve + ping all 24 Meta hosts

Tap any tile; tap "Close" (top right of the panel) to return.

docs.title: Suggested first lap
docs.text:
1. About / System — confirm the app can see your device correctly. If this says "Non-Quest Android device" you're probably running it on a regular Android phone for development (that's fine).

  2. Diagnostics — press "Re-run" once. You'll hear the controllers buzz at the end — three short pulses if everything passed, a specific pattern if anything failed. Then try the Build Tools → Haptic test widget to feel every pattern deliberately.

  3. System Internals — scroll through. The amber-tinted sections ("Security patch gap", "Build-host leak") are findings we surfaced during reverse-engineering. On a Quest 2 running the 2026 builds, the vendor SPL gap is typically ~8 years.

  4. Meta Hosts Audit — tap and watch the categorized list populate. If "Internal" hosts are NOT reachable, that's correct and expected. If any of them resolve, that's a surprise worth investigating.

  5. AI Companion — first launch shows a config form. Give your assistant a name, pick a backend, paste an API key you already have, write a system prompt. Save → chat.

  6. Updates — hit it once. Should say "You're on the latest."

docs.title: Giving permissions
docs.text:
Depending on the panels you use, Android may ask for permissions:

  • Install unknown apps — needed once for the Updates panel's "Install" button to work. Grant to QuestClassic in Settings → Apps → Install unknown apps → QuestClassic.
  • Query all packages — declared in the manifest; granted automatically on install.
  • Internet, network state, vibrate, wake lock — normal permissions, no prompt.

Explicit list in reference/permissions.md.

docs.title: Where state lives
docs.text:
• AI Companion config (name, backend, API key, system prompt) → DataStore at /data/data/io.github.questclassic.app/datastore/ai_config.preferences_pb. Excluded from Android cloud backup by data_extraction_rules.xml.
  • Nothing else is persisted between launches in v0.1.0. Quick note is intentionally ephemeral.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• User guide — read about each panel in depth.
  • contributing/getting-started.md — if you want to write your own panel.
  • Troubleshooting — if something isn't right.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Install QuestClassic on your Meta Quest
docs.text: Five-minute path from a fresh headset to the app running in your Library.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A Meta Quest 2, Quest Pro, Quest 3S, or Quest 3 that's set up and signed in.
  • A PC with adb installed (any OS; brew install android-platform-tools on macOS, apt install adb on Debian/Ubuntu, SDK Platform Tools zip on Windows).
  • A USB-C cable that supports data (not just charging).
  • A Meta Developer account — free, takes 2 minutes. See enable-developer-mode.md.

docs.title: Step 1 — Enable Developer Mode
docs.text: If you've never put a sideloaded app on your headset: follow enable-developer-mode.md, then come back here. This is a one-time thing per account.

docs.title: Step 2 — Enable USB debugging on the headset
docs.text:
With the headset on and awake:

  1. Open Settings → System → Developer.
  2. Turn on USB Connection Dialog.
  3. Turn on ADB.

docs.title: Step 3 — Plug in and authorize
docs.text:
Plug the USB-C cable into your PC and then into the headset. Put the headset on — you'll see a dialog asking if you want to Allow USB debugging from this computer. Tick Always allow and accept.

Confirm the connection from your PC:

adb devices

You should see one line that ends with device (not unauthorized).

docs.title: Step 4 — Download the APK
docs.text: From the latest GitHub Release, download app-release-unsigned.apk (or app-debug.apk if you built it yourself; see contributing/getting-started.md).

docs.title: Step 5 — Install
docs.text:
adb install app-release-unsigned.apk

Expected output ends with Success. If you've installed a previous version:

adb install -r app-release-unsigned.apk      # keeps existing data
adb install -r -d app-release-unsigned.apk   # allow version-code downgrade

docs.title: Step 6 — Open it
docs.text: On the headset: Library → Apps → ▾ dropdown → Unknown Sources → QuestClassic. First launch takes about a second to come up.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Something not working? getting-started/troubleshooting.md.

docs.title: Uninstalling
docs.text:
• From the headset: Library → Unknown Sources → QuestClassic → ⋮ → Uninstall.
  • From ADB: adb uninstall io.github.questclassic.app.

No system state is changed; uninstall is complete.

Last reviewed against QuestClassic v0.1.0.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: In order of "most common first."

docs.title: adb devices says unauthorized
docs.text: You didn't accept the USB-debugging prompt on the headset. Put the headset on, you'll see it immediately — tap Always allow from this computer, then OK. Re-run adb devices; should say device.

docs.title: adb devices is empty
docs.text:
• Cable isn't a data cable. Try another USB-C cable (not the charger-only one that came with your headset).
  • USB debugging isn't enabled on the headset — walk back through install.md step 2.
  • Developer mode isn't on for your account — enable-developer-mode.md.
  • adb server is confused — adb kill-server && adb start-server fixes it 80 % of the time.

docs.title: INSTALL_FAILED_UPDATE_INCOMPATIBLE
docs.text:
You have a previous QuestClassic installed with a different signing key. Reinstall over it:

adb uninstall io.github.questclassic.app
adb install app-release-unsigned.apk

You'll lose your DataStore (AI config). That's fine on a first-install drift; annoying later when we start publishing signed releases alongside the unsigned ones. Once signed releases are stable (see issue #11), pick signed-or-unsigned-and-stick-with-it.

docs.title: INSTALL_FAILED_VERSION_DOWNGRADE
docs.text:
You're trying to install an older version over a newer one. Add -d:

adb install -r -d app-release-unsigned.apk

docs.title: App installs but doesn't appear in the headset Library
docs.text: Look in Library → Apps → ▾ dropdown → Unknown Sources. Meta hides sideloaded apps there by default.

docs.title: App opens but the UI is 2D, not immersive
docs.text: Correct. QuestClassic v0.1.0 is a 2D panel app that runs inside your Horizon home. The AR Home activity is the one experimental immersive surface; the rest live in the standard Quest 2D-panel window. The nostalgic retro look is intentional — early Oculus Home was 2D panels too.

docs.title: Diagnostics buzzed but I don't know what the pattern meant
docs.text:
Count the beats: short = dot, long = dash. Match against reference/buzz-patterns.md. Common ones:

  • . . . (three short) — self-test passed.
  • - . (dash, dot) — battery below 10 %.
  • - . - . — no validated network connection.

docs.title: Signature Verifier says "insane manifest_size" / "unsupported payload version"
docs.text: The file you picked isn't a Meta OTA, or it's a newer OTA format than we've tested. Verify the file is a .zip, contains META-INF/com/android/otacert and payload.bin, and came from Meta's own update servers.

docs.title: AI Companion returns an API error
docs.text:
• 401 — your key is wrong or expired.
  • 429 — you hit a rate limit; wait a minute.
  • 5xx — provider's having a bad day; retry.
  • The Ollama backend's base URL is wrong — it defaults to http://10.0.0.1:11434; change it in the setup form to whatever hosts your Ollama.

docs.title: Meta Hosts Audit says most things are unreachable
docs.text:
• The headset is offline — check Wi-Fi in Quest settings.
  • Your network blocks ICMP (some corporate / school networks do). DNS resolution may still work; the "resolved" count being nonzero is the real health signal.

docs.title: Update panel never offers a newer version
docs.text: Right-side of the issue: either you ARE on the latest, or the self-updater can't reach api.github.com. Open the Meta Hosts Audit panel — if scontent.xx.fbcdn.net is unreachable too, you're probably offline.

docs.title: "Install" button in Updates does nothing
docs.text: Grant QuestClassic the "Install unknown apps" permission: Settings → Apps → Install unknown apps → QuestClassic → Allow. The first update request ought to pop a system prompt; if it didn't, do it manually.

docs.title: Something else
docs.text: Open an issue using the bug-report template — it asks for your headset model, HorizonOS build (visible in System Internals panel), QuestClassic version, and any buzz patterns that fired.

docs.title: Build flavors & signing
docs.text: QuestClassic has one Gradle module and two build types.

docs.title: debug
docs.text:
• applicationIdSuffix = ".debug" — so debug and release can coexist on the same device.
  • isMinifyEnabled = false.
  • Signed with Android's debug keystore (~/.android/debug.keystore).
  • Used for ./gradlew :app:assembleDebug and the CI build workflow.

docs.title: release
docs.text:
• applicationId = io.github.questclassic.app (no suffix).
  • isMinifyEnabled = true + isShrinkResources = true.
  • ProGuard rules at app/proguard-rules.pro keep the AI backend classes and GitHub release types reflectable.
  • Signed with the release keystore ONLY if the four QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE* environment variables are set. Otherwise falls back to debug-signed.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
See security/signing.md for the full flow. The four env vars:

Env var Source in CI QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE Path written by the "Decode signing keystore" step QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_ALIAS secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_ALIAS QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_PASSWORD secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_PASSWORD

docs.title: Why no flavors
docs.text:
We don't ship free vs premium, prod vs staging, openSource vs proprietary, or any other axis. One flavor keeps the mental model simple and the APK count small.

If v0.2 ships a developer build (unlocked logging, extra panels) it'll be a flavor with its own applicationIdSuffix, e.g. io.github.questclassic.app.dev.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Buzz-pattern catalog
docs.text: Every controller buzz pattern the app can fire, what it means, and the exact timing that drives it.

docs.title: Reading a pattern you felt
docs.text:
Every pattern starts with one long burst (~600 ms) — that's the "pattern incoming" marker. After that, count what follows:

  • Short pulse (~80 ms) = dot (.)
  • Long pulse (~240 ms) = dash (-)
  • Short gap inside a letter (~120 ms)
  • Longer gap between letters (~400 ms)

Match the dots/dashes against this table:

Code Pattern Meaning Where it fires ... · · · Self-test passed BuzzPattern.OK (after all Diagnostics tests pass) -. — · Battery below 10 % DiagnosticsEngine.battery -.. — · · Storage below 5 % free DiagnosticsEngine.storage -.-. — · — · No validated network DiagnosticsEngine.network -.- — · — OTA check failed UpdatePanel (reserved; wires up with a planned refactor) -..- — · · — Controller tracking lost Reserved — needs vendor HAL access we don't currently have -- — — Thermal throttling / low memory DiagnosticsEngine.performance ...- · · · — Display fault Reserved

docs.title: Timing constants
docs.text:
val dot        = 80L   // ms
val dash       = 240L
val gap        = 120L   // inside a letter
val longGap    = 400L   // between letters
val startBurst = 600L   // the "pattern incoming" marker

Changing these should be deliberate — users calibrate to them. If you tune one, update this table and run the Build Tools → Haptic test widget to feel every pattern.

docs.title: Why these patterns specifically
docs.text:
• Short codes are short to read.
  • Distinguishable at first touch — -. (BATTERY_LOW) vs -.. (STORAGE_FULL) is hard to mix up because the second one is noticeably longer.
  • **OK is ... ** — three dots is universally "signal received" / "OK" in Morse-adjacent usage.

docs.title: Adding a new pattern
docs.text:
See issue #7. Three steps:

  1. Add a BuzzPattern(...) constant to ControllerHaptics.Companion in app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/core/ControllerHaptics.kt.
  2. Make sure the code-letters are unique (collisions are bad — users identify by feel).
  3. Add a row to the table above.
  4. Wire it up in the panel/engine that detects the condition.

docs.title: Why controllers and not the headset
docs.text:
On Quest 2:

  • The headset has a motor in the strap (VrDeviceManagerServer can access it) but the vendor HAL is signature-gated.
  • The controllers have motors that respond to the standard Android Vibrator API.

So controllers are what a sideloaded app can reach. That's a limitation we chose to work with rather than around; the pattern model works equally well either way.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Icons
docs.text: We use androidx.compose.material.icons.outlined.* exclusively — one visual style, so the home grid reads coherently. The material-icons-extended dep enables everything in the Material catalog.

docs.title: Currently used

docs.title: Choosing an icon for a new panel
docs.text:
• Pick from Icons.Outlined.* — not Filled, not TwoTone, not Rounded, not Sharp. Keeps the grid consistent.
  • Use something semantic — Apps for launching apps, MonitorHeart for diagnostics. Avoid metaphors that need a label to parse.
  • If none fit, write a vector drawable yourself under app/src/main/res/drawable/ — see ic_launcher_foreground.xml as an example — and import it via painterResource.

docs.text: Consistency. The home grid's 2×N tiles form a visual rhythm; mixing Outlined + Filled would break it. If a specific panel really needs a different style (say, Filled for emphasis), use it inside the panel body — not in the tile icon.

material-icons-extended adds ~250 KB. See ADR 0006.

docs.title: AndroidManifest.xml — line by line
docs.text: Our full manifest is ~70 lines. Here's each block, annotated.

docs.title: Permissions
docs.text: See permissions.md.

docs.title: Features
docs.text:
<uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.vr.headtracking" android:required="false" />
<uses-feature android:name="com.oculus.feature.PASSTHROUGH" android:required="false" />
<uses-feature android:name="oculus.software.handtracking" android:required="false" />
  • required="false" on all three — the app installs regardless; features without the backing capability degrade.
  • vr.headtracking — standard Android feature flag for head-tracked devices.
  • com.oculus.feature.PASSTHROUGH — true on Quest 2+ in MR-capable modes.
  • oculus.software.handtracking — true if hand-tracking is on.

docs.title: Supported-devices
docs.text:
<meta-data android:name="com.oculus.supportedDevices"
    android:value="hollywood|monterey|seacliff|eureka|panther" />

Appears twice — once on <application> and once on <activity> for MainActivity. Meta's Library uses whichever it finds first; duplicating is defensive.

docs.title: Application element
docs.text:
<application
    android:name=".QuestClassicApplication"
    android:allowBackup="false"
    android:dataExtractionRules="@xml/data_extraction_rules"
    android:fullBackupContent="false"
    ...
  • allowBackup="false" + dataExtractionRules — belt-and-suspenders against automated cloud backup picking up the AI key DataStore. See architecture/storage.md.
  • fullBackupContent="false" — same reason, for the legacy full-backup path.
  • android:icon="@mipmap/ic_launcher" — adaptive icon (vector drawable background + foreground).

docs.title: MainActivity
docs.text:
<activity android:name=".MainActivity"
    android:exported="true"
    android:launchMode="singleTask"
    android:configChanges="keyboard|keyboardHidden|navigation|orientation|screenLayout|screenSize|uiMode"
    android:theme="@style/Theme.QuestClassic">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
        <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
        <category android:name="com.oculus.intent.category.VR" />
    </intent-filter>
</activity>
  • exported="true" — needed on Android 12+ for any activity that has an <intent-filter>.
  • launchMode="singleTask" — the app only ever has one task; subsequent launches reuse it.
  • configChanges=… — we handle these ourselves (we're Compose, no need to recreate on a keyboard open).
  • Dual LAUNCHER + VR categories — surfaces in both standard Android launchers and Meta's Library.

docs.title: ARHomeActivity
docs.text:
<activity android:name=".ar.ARHomeActivity"
    android:exported="false"
    android:launchMode="singleTask"
    android:configChanges="keyboard|keyboardHidden|navigation|orientation|screenLayout|screenSize|uiMode|density"
    android:theme="@style/Theme.QuestClassic"
    android:resizeableActivity="false" />
  • exported="false" — only MainActivity launches it.
  • resizeableActivity="false" — when we add real passthrough, we don't want the system packing us into a 2D panel window.
  • density in configChanges — handling display-density changes without recreating is cheap and smooth.

docs.title: FileProvider (for Updates)
docs.text:
<provider
    android:name="androidx.core.content.FileProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.updates"
    android:exported="false"
    android:grantUriPermissions="true">
    <meta-data android:name="android.support.FILE_PROVIDER_PATHS"
        android:resource="@xml/file_provider_paths" />
</provider>
  • authorities = "${applicationId}.updates" — namespaced by package ID so debug and release builds don't collide (applicationIdSuffix=".debug" in debug build).
  • grantUriPermissions="true" — needed to hand the downloaded APK URI to the system package installer.
  • res/xml/file_provider_paths.xml grants only cache-path name="updates" — the installer can read our update APK, nothing else.

docs.title: AndroidX Startup
docs.text:
<provider
    android:name="androidx.startup.InitializationProvider"
    android:authorities="${applicationId}.androidx-startup"
    android:exported="false"
    tools:node="merge" />

Pulled in transitively by WorkManager / lifecycle-runtime even when we don't use the AppStartup DSL. Harmless; required for those libs' init on some Android versions.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.
