docs.title: ProGuard / R8 rules
docs.text:
Our rules file is small and focused. In app/proguard-rules.pro:

-keep class io.github.questclassic.app.ai.** { *; }
-keepclassmembers class io.github.questclassic.app.update.GithubRelease { *; }
-keepclassmembers class io.github.questclassic.app.update.GithubAsset { *; }
-dontwarn org.codehaus.mojo.animal_sniffer.IgnoreJRERequirement

docs.title: What each line does
docs.text:
• -keep class io.github.questclassic.app.ai.** { *; } Keeps every class under app.ai.* with all members. R8 could otherwise rename ClaudeBackend → a$b$c and break the kotlinx.serialization wire types that use reflection-ish property discovery at runtime. Since we have three backends and the AI panel's picker lists them via reflection-friendly backendById, we keep them visible.

  • -keepclassmembers class …GithubRelease { *; } + GithubAsset Keeps the field names of the two JSON wire types kotlinx.serialization reads from GitHub. If R8 renamed browser_download_url to a, deserialization would fail at runtime.

  • -dontwarn org.codehaus.mojo.animal_sniffer.IgnoreJRERequirement Suppresses a benign warning emitted by OkHttp's internal use of a shaded animal_sniffer annotation that's not on our classpath.

docs.title: Why so little
docs.text:
• Our serialization is kotlinx.serialization with @Serializable — codegen-based, not reflection-based, so most classes don't need -keep.
  • Our DI container is hand-wired — no reflection discovery to protect.
  • Compose compiler generates its own metadata and handles its own keeps.

docs.title: When to add a rule
docs.text:
• You're using a new library that fails at runtime in a release build.
  • You added a class that's instantiated by name (reflection or JNI).
  • Adding a @Keep annotation to the class works too and localizes the rule; prefer that where possible.

docs.title: Testing R8 output
docs.text:
./gradlew :app:assembleRelease
# Inspect:
./gradlew :app:analyzeReleaseBundle    # if bundle analyzer is wired
unzip -l app/build/outputs/apk/release/app-release.apk | head

If something crashes in release but works in debug, R8 almost certainly stripped something; look in app/build/outputs/mapping/release/ for the mapping file and reverse the trace.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Root detection — the signals we check
docs.text:
QuestClassic's root detection lives in core/RootDetector.kt. It inspects five signals on first query and memoises the result.

Signal What we look for Value if hit suOnPath su binary at any of 10 standard paths: /system/bin/su, /system/xbin/su, /sbin/su, /data/local/su, /data/local/bin/su, /data/local/xbin/su, /system/sd/xbin/su, /system/bin/failsafe/su, /su/bin/su, /vendor/bin/su true → classical Android root magiskPathsPresent Any of /data/adb/magisk, /data/adb/magisk.db, /data/adb/modules, /sbin/.magisk, /cache/.disable_magisk true → Magisk installed systemWritable Can create a benign canary file at /system/.qc_root_probe true → /system has been remounted RW testKeysBuild Build.TAGS contains test-keys true → signed with developer test keys, not retail debuggableBuild Build.TYPE is userdebug or eng true → non-production build

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text:
val confidence: Confidence
    get() = when {
        suOnPath && magiskPathsPresent -> Confidence.HIGH
        suOnPath || magiskPathsPresent || systemWritable -> Confidence.MEDIUM
        testKeysBuild || debuggableBuild -> Confidence.LOW
        else -> Confidence.NONE
    }
  • HIGH — two independent root mechanisms both visible. Very safe to run privileged actions.
  • MEDIUM — one strong signal. Safe to run; action may still fail if SELinux is in enforcing mode and blocks a specific syscall.
  • LOW — the build is developer-flagged but no actual root binary is present. QuestClassic treats this as "not rooted" for action purposes; the panel just shows the dev-flag so you know.
  • NONE — stock retail. Panels show dry-run only.

docs.title: What we DO NOT do
docs.text:
1. No su invocation. Running Runtime.exec("su -c ...") is noisy, triggers device policy, and tells you nothing the file check didn't already tell you.
  2. No SafetyNet / Play Integrity attestation. That's Google's cloud attestation; it doesn't tell you anything about root, only about Google's trust model.
  3. No QSEE challenge. That's Meta's business, and we don't impersonate retail apps.
  4. No exploit attempt. QuestClassic detects root; it does not obtain root. See ADR 0009.

docs.title: What the result unlocks
docs.text:
See each panel's user-guide page for the action it enables:

  • Strip Meta
  • Firmware Dump
  • Boot Animation
  • Developer Super-Mode
  • Home Menu Swapper

docs.title: Caching
docs.text: RootDetector memoises status() after the first call. To re-query (after you've just enabled or disabled root), call refresh().

docs.text:

docs.title: API — ai package
docs.text: Pluggable LLM backends behind a one-method interface.

docs.title: AIBackend
docs.text:
sealed interface AIBackend {
    val id: String
    val displayName: String
    suspend fun chat(
        systemPrompt: String,
        history: List<ChatMessage>,
        apiKey: String,
        model: String?,
    ): Result<String>
}

enum class Role { user, assistant, system }
data class ChatMessage(val role: Role, val content: String)
  • chat(...) must return a Result<String> — success = the assistant's reply text; failure = anything that went wrong.
  • model is nullable so backends can fall back to their own default.
  • apiKey is overloaded for Ollama (we repurpose it as the base URL since Ollama doesn't use auth).

docs.title: ClaudeBackend
docs.text:
• id: claude
  • displayName: Claude (Anthropic)
  • endpoint: https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages
  • default model: claude-sonnet-5-5
  • auth: x-api-key: <key> + anthropic-version: 2023-06-01 header
  • request: {model, max_tokens=1024, system, messages: [{role, content}]}
  • extracts first text content from the response

docs.title: OpenAIBackend
docs.text:
• id: openai
  • displayName: OpenAI
  • endpoint: https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions
  • default model: gpt-4o-mini
  • auth: Authorization: Bearer <key>
  • request: {model, messages: [{role, content}], max_tokens=1024}
  • extracts first choices[0].message.content

docs.title: OllamaBackend
docs.text:
• id: ollama
  • displayName: Ollama (local LAN)
  • endpoint: ${base}/api/chat (base supplied by user)
  • default model: llama3.2
  • auth: none
  • request: {model, messages: [{role, content}], stream=false}
  • extracts message.content

docs.title: AIRepository
docs.text:
class AIRepository(context: Context, http: OkHttpClient) {
    val backends: List<AIBackend>
    fun backendById(id: String): AIBackend
    suspend fun load(): AIConfig
    suspend fun save(cfg: AIConfig)
}

data class AIConfig(
    val assistantName: String,
    val backendId: String,
    val model: String,
    val apiKey: String,
    val systemPrompt: String,
)

AIRepository wraps:

  • the backend registry (backends),
  • DataStore-backed config persistence,
  • a backendById lookup that never returns null (falls back to the first registered backend).

docs.title: Adding a new backend
docs.text:
1. Create app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ai/GeminiBackend.kt.
  2. Implement AIBackend.
  3. Register in AIRepository.backends.
  4. It appears in the backend picker automatically.

See issue #6 for a good first issue version.

docs.title: What we don't do here
docs.text:
• No conversation memory beyond what the user types in one session. (Chat history cleared on panel close.)
  • No streaming. We wait for the full response before adding it to the history. Streaming is tracked informally for a future PR.
  • No tool use. Models can't call our code; this is pure chat.
  • No caching. Every chat(...) is a fresh HTTP request.

docs.title: PayloadVerifier
docs.text:
class PayloadVerifier(context: Context) {
    suspend fun verify(archiveUri: Uri): Result<Report>

    data class Report(
        val archiveName: String,
        val payloadSize: Long,
        val manifestSize: Long,
        val metaSigSize: Int,
        val signaturesOffset: Long,
        val signaturesSize: Int,
        val metadataDigestHex: String,
        val finalDigestHex: String,
        val metadataSignatureValid: Boolean,
        val finalSignatureValid: Boolean,
        val certSubject: String,
        val certIssuer: String,
        val certNotAfter: String,
        val certSha256Fingerprint: String,
    ) {
        val allGood: Boolean
    }
}
  • verify(uri) reads the picked .zip streaming, extracts payload.bin and META-INF/com/android/otacert from the ZIP's central directory on the fly.
  • Returns a Result — success Report or a captured Throwable.
  • Zero-dep: pure Java crypto + our own varint parser.

See user-guide/signature-verifier.md for the UX and reverse-engineering/ota-format.md for the format background.

docs.title: MetaHostsAudit
docs.text:
object MetaHostsAudit {
    enum class Category { AUTH, GRAPH, GENAI, PAYMENTS, CDN, INTERNAL }

    data class Host(val name: String, val category: Category, val note: String = "")
    data class Probe(val host: Host, val ip: String?, val reachable: Boolean, val latencyMs: Long?, val error: String?)

    val all: List<Host>
    suspend fun probe(host: Host, timeoutMs: Int = 1500): Probe

docs.text:
Every public suspend function here uses withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { … } internally. Callers don't need to switch dispatchers themselves.

docs.title: API — os package
docs.text: Read-only device introspection. Everything here uses android.os.Build + reflection into android.os.SystemProperties — same values Settings → About and adb shell getprop return.

docs.title: DeviceIntrospection
docs.text:
class DeviceIntrospection(context: Context) {
    data class Prop(val key: String, val value: String?)

    fun summary(): List<Prop>
    val isQuest: Boolean
}

Powers the About panel. Returns a curated list of 13 properties, in display order, for the summary card.

docs.title: SystemPropertyProbe
docs.text:
class SystemPropertyProbe {
    fun get(key: String): String?
    val summary: String
}

Powers the System Internals panel. Lets a Composable call probe.get("ro.build.branch") for any system property; returns null if the property doesn't exist or is empty.

docs.title: Why reflection
docs.text:
android.os.SystemProperties is a hidden API — public SDK stubs don't expose it. Both classes here reach it via:

val method = Class.forName("android.os.SystemProperties").getMethod("get", String::class.java)
val value  = method.invoke(null, key) as? String

This is permitted on Android 11+ without the warn-logs-and-eventually-blocks hidden-API restrictions because SystemProperties.get(String) is in the "greylist-max-o" (unrestricted) bucket. We do NOT read non-public setters or restricted properties.

docs.title: What we never read
docs.text:
• Properties under persist.vendor.* that could include device secrets (we read none of them).
  • Properties under ro.serialno or ril.serialnumber (we don't need the device serial for anything).
  • Nothing that requires elevated capabilities or hidden API bypass flags.

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• On some Android versions SystemProperties.get for a non-existent key returns "" (empty string); we normalize to null.
  • Properties can change between reads (e.g. ro.vendor.build.security_patch is immutable, but persist.* ones are mutable). Our panels snapshot once per open.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: API — update package
docs.text: SelfUpdater + its wire types.

docs.title: SelfUpdater
docs.text:
class SelfUpdater(context: Context, http: OkHttpClient) {
    suspend fun checkLatest(): GithubRelease?
    fun pickApk(release: GithubRelease): GithubAsset?
    fun isNewer(release: GithubRelease): Boolean
    suspend fun downloadApk(asset: GithubAsset): File?
    fun install(apk: File)

    companion object {
        const val OWNER = "REPLACE_WITH_OWNER"   // rewritten at release time by CI
        const val REPO = "QuestClassic"
    }
}

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
val release = container.updater.checkLatest() ?: return
if (container.updater.isNewer(release)) {
    val asset = container.updater.pickApk(release) ?: return
    val file = container.updater.downloadApk(asset) ?: return
    container.updater.install(file)
}

docs.title: checkLatest()
docs.text:
• HTTP GET https://api.github.com/repos/$OWNER/$REPO/releases/latest
  • Headers: Accept: application/vnd.github+json
  • Deserialize via kotlinx.serialization with ignoreUnknownKeys = true.
  • Returns null on any non-2xx, non-JSON, or unparseable response.

docs.title: pickApk(release)
docs.text: Picks the first asset whose name ends with .apk (case-insensitive). If a release has multiple APKs (e.g. we add arm64 + universal later), the picker will need to get smarter.

docs.title: isNewer(release)
docs.text: Strips a leading v from both release.tag_name and BuildConfig.VERSION_NAME, then calls compareSemver. Returns true iff the release version strictly exceeds the installed version.

docs.title: compareSemver(a, b) (internal)
docs.text:
Simple component-wise numeric compare on ./--split pieces. Non-numeric components are treated as 0.

  • "1.0.0" vs "0.9.0" → 1
  • "1.0.0" vs "1.0.0" → 0
  • "1.0.0-rc.1" vs "1.0.0" → 0 (treats rc as 0; good enough for v0, see issue #12)

docs.title: downloadApk(asset)
docs.text:
• HTTP GET asset.browser_download_url
  • Streams to cacheDir/questclassic-update.apk
  • Returns the File on success, null on any failure.

docs.title: install(apk)
docs.text:
• Builds a FileProvider URI with authority ${applicationId}.updates.
  • Starts Intent.ACTION_VIEW with application/vnd.android.package-archive + FLAG_GRANT_READ_URI_PERMISSION + FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK.
  • Android's system package installer takes over.
  • First time, the user is prompted to grant "Install unknown apps" to QuestClassic.

docs.title: Wire types
docs.text:
@Serializable
data class GithubAsset(val name: String, val browser_download_url: String, val size: Long)

@Serializable
data class GithubRelease(
    val tag_name: String,
    val name: String? = null,
    val prerelease: Boolean = false,
    val assets: List<GithubAsset> = emptyList(),
    val body: String? = null,
)

snake_case because that's what GitHub's REST API emits. Keeping them that way (vs renaming with @SerialName) makes the types traceable one-to-one with GitHub's release schema.

docs.title: Owner/repo rewrite at CI time
docs.text:
release.yml runs:

sed -i "s|REPLACE_WITH_OWNER|${{ github.repository_owner }}|g" SelfUpdater.kt
sed -i "s|\"QuestClassic\"|\"${{ github.event.repository.name }}\"|g" SelfUpdater.kt

So a fork gets its own release channel without any code edits. Same reason we keep the constants in a companion object (easy to sed) rather than a build-config field (would need Gradle to know the owner).

docs.title: AVB chain of trust
docs.text: Android Verified Boot 2.0 as it runs on Meta Quest 2, end to end.

docs.title: The chain
docs.text:
Qualcomm on-die fuses (Meta OEM fuse set)
  └─ PBL verifies XBL
      └─ XBL verifies ABL (signed by `abl_signing_keys:release`)
          └─ ABL loads `boot.img` and `vbmeta`
              └─ vbmeta verifies:
                  ├─ boot.img                (hash descriptor)
                  ├─ recovery.img            (hash descriptor)
                  ├─ dtbo.img                (hash descriptor)
                  ├─ chain → vbmeta_system   (rollback_index_location=1)
                  │   ├─ hashtree(system)
                  │   ├─ hashtree(system_ext)
                  │   └─ hashtree(product)
                  └─ chain → vbmeta_vendor   (rollback_index_location=2)
                      ├─ hashtree(vendor)
                      └─ hashtree(odm)

Every signature is RSA-2048+SHA-256 against Meta's AOSP_Release_Pub cert (or a key chained from it). The cert is in META-INF/com/android/otacert in every OTA; its fingerprint is burned into the device during manufacturing.

docs.title: The root cert
docs.text:
• Subject: CN=AOSP_Release_Pub, O=Oculus, OU=Miramar, L=Menlo Park, ST=CA, C=US, emailAddress=security@oculus.com.
  • Issuer: CN=AOSP_Int_Pub (Meta's internal intermediate CA).
  • Validity: 2019-11-08 → 2029-11-05. Non-trivial: Meta needs to roll this before Nov 2029.
  • Public key: RSA-2048.
  • Serial: 6.
  • Signature algorithm: sha256WithRSAEncryption.
  • SHA-256 fingerprint: B8:C9:D2:8A:61:6F:83:14:85:C2:3F:13:6D:AB:91:B0:91:C9:9A:A0:3D:CA:57:08:1A:25:D1:4F:3B:C1:9F:A1.

docs.title: vbmeta descriptors
docs.text:
Root vbmeta carries:

Descriptor For Digest hash boot (34,209,792 B) 4240e18b03c55579eba e94f4332509c6… hash recovery (48,070,656 B) e36aba8719a1df2353 eba4e18ff090df… hash dtbo (1,181,768 B) b02825c0571676fac2 95b5875db0e9fe… chain_partition vbmeta_system (rb_loc=1) separate RSA-2048 pubkey chain_partition vbmeta_vendor (rb_loc=2) separate RSA-2048 pubkey

Plus a stack of property descriptors with com.android.build.*.os_version, .fingerprint, .security_patch — these are where the internal Meta build-host hostname leaks into AVB-signed metadata (F-03 in the firmware review).

vbmeta_system and vbmeta_vendor have their own public keys (signed by the root) and each carries hashtree descriptors for their partitions. Hashtree digests are SHA-1 (the F-02 in the firmware review).

docs.title: Rollback index
docs.text: Each vbmeta has a rollback_index value (1788652800 on our build = early 2027 timestamp). The device stores a per-slot rollback counter in a tamper-evident area; it refuses to boot an OTA whose rollback_index is lower than what the device has seen. Prevents downgrading to a known-vulnerable older build.

docs.title: What breaks the chain
docs.text:
• Modifying any byte of any verified partition → dm-verity hashtree mismatch → vbmeta fails → bootloader refuses.
  • Replacing a partition with a differently-signed one → vbmeta chain_partition cert doesn't match → fail.
  • Flashing an older OTA → rollback_index check fails → refuses.
  • Replacing vbmeta itself with a different signer's → root RSA check fails against the fused cert → fail.

docs.title: What you cannot modify at all
docs.text:
• The on-die fuses (they're OTP — one-time-programmable).
  • The PBL (in ROM).
  • XBL and ABL without a Meta signing key.
  • Any of the verified partitions without breaking dm-verity.

docs.title: Where the bootloader-unlock conversation ends
docs.text:
Meta's bootloader on retail Quest 2 has no fastboot flashing unlock equivalent. Even on dev-mode-enabled accounts, there's no path to tell the bootloader "trust my new vbmeta." Historical Quest jailbreak work targeted specific Qualcomm/Oculus vulnerabilities in older firmware; the current build has those patched.

So: a sideloaded APK (like QuestClassic) coexists with Meta's signed system; a custom ROM would need either (a) a new unpatched exploit chain or (b) Meta's signing key. Neither is in scope for this project.

docs.title: Meta auth flow
docs.text: How the headset proves its identity to Meta's backend, and how your user account is layered on top of that.

docs.title: Two layers, in parallel
docs.text:
Device auth — proves "this is a real Meta Quest 2 with factory keybox N." User auth — proves "this is user X signing in with their Meta account."

Every request to Meta's graph carries BOTH tokens. The backend can reject either independently.

docs.title: Who holds the private key
docs.text:
Qualcomm's Keybox, installed at manufacture by vendor.oculus.hardware.keyboxinstaller@1.0-service. The private key lives in TrustZone-protected secure storage — Android userspace can never read it. DeviceAuth talks to it over RPC via:

  • oculus.internal.cms.ICMHeadsetRpc (cms_hmd_rpc) — headset side
  • oculus.internal.cms.ICMControllerRpc (cms_ctrl_rpc) — controllers

"CMS" = Credential Management System, the TrustZone trusted-app that owns the key.

docs.title: Challenge/response protocol
docs.text:
1. DeviceChallengeFetcher.fetchChallenge(): 
    POST https://graph.facebook-hardware.com/…
{ auth_protocol_version: 1,
  access_token: DEVICE_AUTH_SERVICE_ACCESS_TOKEN,
  device_certificate: <pem>,
  supported_algorithms: [SHA256withRSA, SHA384withRSA, SHA512withRSA] }
→ { challenge, signature_algorithm }
  2. DeviceAuth hands the challenge bytes to CMS via ICMHeadsetRpc. Signing happens inside QSEE. The signature comes back to Android userspace.
  3. Login with the signed challenge: 
    POST https://graph.facebook-hardware.com/…
LoginChallenge { device_id, device_type, nonce, signature }
→ { device_access_token, expiration_time_absolute }

docs.title: Caching + refresh
docs.text:
• Tokens cached in DeviceAuthStore (device-protected storage, available before user unlock).
  • DeviceAccessTokenExtendJobService refreshes 10 min before expiry.
  • On refresh: broadcasts com.oculus.deviceauthservice.NEW_TOKEN_AVAILABLE; every client rereads.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text:
• HARDWARE_AUTH__DEVICE_NOT_REGISTERED = 2699001 — re-register the device cert.
  • HARDWARE_AUTH__REAUTH_REQUIRED = 2699012 — full challenge/response again.

docs.title: Rate limiting
docs.text: HTTP 400/401/500 trip a ConcurrentRequestThrottleQueue on the client — client-side rate limit to avoid hammering the backend when it's complaining.

docs.title: Where the account state lives
docs.text:
A Room SQLite CapabilitiesDatabase with entities:

Account                         — Meta accounts signed in
ActiveUser                      — which one is current
Application                     — every installed Meta/3P app
Capability                      — feature flags
CapabilityTag                   — grouping
AccountCapability               — join account ↔ capability
AccountApplicationCapability    — join account ↔ app ↔ capability

So on-device there's a materialized {user × app × capability} matrix — queried before anything tries to do anything privileged.

docs.title: Broadcast-driven workers
docs.text:
IdentityManagementServiceReceiver listens for:

  • android.intent.action.BOOT_COMPLETED
  • com.oculus.horizon.ACCESS_TOKEN_CHANGED — key signal

On each, schedules a constellation of WorkManager jobs:

AccessTokenWorker                              refresh user token
UserIdentityContextWorker                      who am I right now
CapabilitiesQueryWorker                        what can the device do
UserAccountCapabilitiesQueryWorker             what can THIS user do
UserAccountApplicationGroupingCapabilitiesQueryWorker   per-app perms
SyncPreferencesStoreWorker                     sync settings
SalsaWorker                                    (unknown Meta codename)
NeutralAgeGateWorker                           age-gate / COPPA check

Periodic job runs every 15 min to keep it fresh.

docs.title: Hardcoded Meta-domain recognition
docs.text:
For OAuth callback trust:

facebook.com, facebook-hardware.com, facebookstudy.com,
facebookvirtualassistant.com, instagram.com

docs.title: Known cross-app identity package allow-list
docs.text:
FACEBOOK_HORIZON_DEV / RC / RELEASE_TEST / STABLE / STAGING
INSTAGRAM_INHOUSE / PROD / PRODV2 / PROD_K1 / PROD_SET

If those specific Facebook/Instagram builds are installed on the headset, they share auth state with HorizonOS. On retail they aren't — but the handshake is wired.

docs.title: The MVAN supervision layer
docs.text:
MVAN = Meta's supervised / teen-account enforcement system. Pieces:

  • MVanDatabase — Room DB for MVAN state.
  • MVanServiceReceiver — triggers.
  • MVanScreenTimeUploadWorker — uploads screen-time usage to Meta.
  • MvanLaunchRestrictionDataQuery — "can this user launch this app right now?" Runs before every app launch.
  • NeutralAgeGateActions / NeutralAgeGateWorker — Meta's name for the age-verification flow.
  • Dialog permissions: SHOW_MVAN_LAUNCH_RESTRICTED_DIALOG, SHOW_MVAN_SOCIAL_RESTRICTED_DIALOG, SHOW_LOGIN_WITH_TWILIGHT_DIALOG_ACTIVITY.
  • "Twilight" = login-dialog flavor for supervised accounts.

Enforcement runs server-side AND cached client-side (CapabilitiesDatabase) — can't be bypassed offline.

docs.title: End-to-end sign-in sequence
docs.text:
0.  init → trackingservice, orchestrator, xrspd, parfait up
1.  DeviceAuthService.onCreate — DeviceAuthStore loaded (empty on factory reset)
2.  First caller requests device token
    ↓
    DeviceChallengeFetcher.fetchChallenge — POST graph.facebook-hardware.com
    ↓
    DeviceAuth hands challenge to QSEE via ICMHeadsetRpc
    ↓
    QSEE signs with factory keybox key
    ↓
    POST graph.facebook-hardware.com (LoginChallenge + signature)
    ← device_access_token + expiration
    ↓
    DeviceAuthStore cached, NEW_TOKEN_AVAILABLE broadcast, 10-min pre-expiry refresh scheduled
3.  VrShell draws FirstTimeNuxHollywood
4.  AccountsCenterPWA opens accountscenter.meta.com
    User signs in; DAT in request headers
    ↓
    (optional) CompanionServer accepts account from phone companion
5.  User access token returned
    Broadcast ACCESS_TOKEN_CHANGED
    ↓
    IdentityManagement starts workers, populates CapabilitiesDatabase
    ↓
    Periodic 15-min job scheduled
6.  NeutralAgeGateWorker runs
7.  If supervised: MVAN workers start
8.  Every graph.* request now carries both tokens
9.  Horizon Platform providers come up
10. Headset at Home

docs.title: Why this is unusually robust
docs.text:
• Device cert in TrustZone — rooting Android doesn't expose it.
  • User token requires device token — can't be replayed from a non-Quest client.
  • Tokens auto-expire; can be revoked — Meta can nuke a specific keybox.
  • Supervised restrictions enforced both server + client — can't be bypassed offline.

That's also why there's no realistic path to using a Meta account on a Quest 2 without a working device cert — you'd have to compromise QSEE, which is the hard problem all Qualcomm-TrustZone research has been trying for years.

docs.title: OTA format
docs.text: Everything that's in a Meta Quest 2 OTA .zip, byte-level and structurally. Based on AOSP's A/B update_engine CrAU v2 format; Meta uses it unchanged.

docs.title: ZIP layout
docs.text:
q2_<build>.zip
├── q2_<build>/
│   ├── META-INF/com/android/
│   │   ├── metadata                    text pre/post-condition
│   │   ├── metadata.pb                 same, as protobuf
│   │   └── otacert                     PEM X.509, OTA signing cert
│   ├── apex_info.pb                    list of APEX modules in target
│   ├── care_map.pb                     per-partition blocks-in-use + fingerprints
│   ├── payload.bin                     ~1.1 GB CrAU payload
│   └── payload_properties.txt          SHA-256 + size of payload + its metadata prefix
└── __MACOSX/                           AppleDouble metadata (someone opened it on a Mac)

The __MACOSX prefix shows this specific ZIP was repacked on a Mac at some point; not part of the original Meta pipeline.

docs.title: payload.bin header (first 24 bytes)
docs.text:
Offset Bytes Meaning Value on this OTA 0 4 magic CrAU 4 8 version (uint64 BE) 2 12 8 manifest_size 86,663 20 4 metadata_signature_size (v2+) 267

Next 86,663 bytes = the DeltaArchiveManifest protobuf. Next 267 bytes = the metadata Signatures protobuf. Next ~1.1 GB = data blobs. Final 267 bytes = the final Signatures protobuf.

docs.title: DeltaArchiveManifest (abridged)
docs.text:
AOSP's update_metadata.proto:

Field # Name Why we care 3 block_size 4096 on this device 4 signatures_offset 1,102,976,859 (bytes from data_blobs_start) 5 signatures_size 267 12 minor_version 0 (full OTA, no delta ops) 13 partitions (repeated) 25 entries on this OTA 14 max_timestamp 1,793,760,311 = anti-rollback floor 15 dynamic_partition_metadata super cap 6.44 GB, group kona_dynamic_partitions 17 apex_info (repeated) 0 here; APEX info lives in sidecar apex_info.pb 18 security_patch_level 2026-09-06

Each PartitionUpdate has:

  • partition_name (string)
  • new_partition_info { size, hash }
  • operations (repeated InstallOperation)

Operation types in our build (full OTA, so no diff ops):

Type Count Compression REPLACE_XZ 1439 xz REPLACE_BZ 52 bz2 REPLACE 16 raw

25 partitions × 1507 ops × 3.13 GB logical → 1.10 GB on-disk = 35% compression.

docs.title: Metadata signature
docs.text:
Standard CrAU-v2:

  • SHA-256 over bytes [0 .. 24 + manifest_size) = first 86,687 bytes.
  • RSA-2048 signature in a Signatures protobuf, 267 bytes total.
Signatures {
  signatures: [Signature {
    version: deprecated
    data: <256 bytes RSA sig>
    unpadded_signature_size: 256
  }]
}

docs.title: Final payload signature
docs.text:
The one that trips up every first-time implementer. AOSP hashes:

[0 .. 24 + manifest_size) ∪ [data_blobs_start .. final_sig_at)

That is: header + manifest AND THEN data section up to the final signature blob — the 267 bytes of metadata signature in between are skipped. Why: those bytes aren't persisted to disk during install; the device computes the hash over what it writes, not over what it discards.

Reproduce in Python:

h = hashlib.sha256()
h.update(payload[:24 + manifest_size])
h.update(payload[data_blobs_start:final_sig_at])
expected_hash = h.digest()

Reproduce in Kotlin (what we do in PayloadVerifier):

val md = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
// Part 1: header + manifest
f.seek(0); streamToDigest(f, 24 + manifestSize, md)
// Part 2: data section up to the sig
f.seek(dataBlobsStart); streamToDigest(f, finalSigStart - dataBlobsStart, md)
val digest = md.digest()

docs.title: Sidecar files
docs.text:
• apex_info.pb — list of APEX modules + versions in the target image. On this build: 30 APEXes, almost all pinned to the Android 14 QPR module-release train 340090000.
  • care_map.pb — per-partition "blocks in use" map + per-partition fingerprints (where the internal build-host leak lives).
  • metadata.pb — binary form of the metadata text file.
  • otacert — PEM X.509 signing cert.
  • payload_properties.txt — FILE_HASH=…, FILE_SIZE=…, METADATA_HASH=…, METADATA_SIZE=…. Useful for cheap integrity checks before even parsing the payload.

docs.title: Review bar for adding a dependency
docs.text:
A PR that adds a new dependency gets more scrutiny than one that adds code. Questions the PR must answer:

  1. Is this a maintained library? First-party AndroidX, JetBrains, Square, Google — yes. One-person GitHub repos — only if trivially auditable.
  2. What's its APK-size impact? Run ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease before and after; note the diff.
  3. What's its transitive-dep footprint? ./gradlew :app:dependencies diff.
  4. Does it do any network calls at startup? No. If yes, hard block unless there's an opt-out.
  5. Does it embed native libraries? If yes, which architectures, how big?
  6. Does it do reflection on hidden Android APIs? If yes, needs manual review per Android version.
  7. License? Apache 2.0 / MIT / BSD-3-Clause — fine. GPL — case-by-case; LGPL only if we can .so-link (we're Kotlin, so this matters less).

docs.text:

Dependabot runs on the repo (will be enabled in the first follow-up PR); PRs get reviewed like any other.
