docs.title: Emulation FAQ — "why can't you just run it in QEMU?"
docs.text:
Short answer: because the Quest 2 refuses to boot anything that isn't signed by keys that aren't in any emulator and can't be pulled out of the device.

Long answer below, in plain English, then in detail.

docs.title: In one paragraph
docs.text: A modern phone-class Qualcomm chip boots in stages. The very first stage is burned into the silicon itself — not firmware you can replace, actual gates in the die. That first stage refuses to hand control to anything that isn't signed by Qualcomm. Qualcomm, in turn, signs a loader that only runs a Meta-signed loader. Meta's loader only runs a Meta-signed kernel. Each stage verifies the next against a key, and those keys ultimately trace back to fuses that were blown at the factory. An emulator has no fuses. Which means no emulator has the "I am a real Quest 2" credential the next stage is looking for. End of story — until someone finds a bug in one of the stages, which is what the entire mobile-security research community does for a living, and which stays patched when they succeed.

docs.title: Why the first stage won't run under QEMU
docs.text:
The Snapdragon XR2 Gen 1 (platform codename kona, the same base chip in the Quest 2) has what Qualcomm calls a Primary Boot Loader (PBL) in on-die ROM. Its job is to:

  1. Sanity-check the device state.
  2. Look at the boot partition and find a Qualcomm-signed loader (XBL).
  3. Verify XBL's signature against a root hash stored in fuses on the die.
  4. If verification succeeds, jump to XBL. If it fails, halt.

A fuse is a one-time-programmable element in the silicon. After the fuse is blown at factory, its state is physically embedded in the chip. QEMU has no fuses. You can emulate a Snapdragon's instruction set — ARMv8-A — but you can't emulate "pretend these fuses are set to Qualcomm's root hash." The fuses aren't a register you flip; they're state the chip reads out of itself.

Which means: even step 1 of the boot chain refuses to proceed on anything that isn't the real silicon.

docs.title: Why the next stages don't help
docs.text:
Suppose someone did find a way to emulate the fuses (they haven't, publicly, on the SM8250 family). The next stages are:

  • XBL (eXtensible Boot Loader) — verifies the Android Boot Loader (ABL) against Meta's signing keys.
  • ABL — verifies the Linux kernel and the Android Verified Boot metadata against Meta's keys.
  • Everything downstream — verifies against AVB.

Meta's private signing keys live in Meta's offline Luleå HSM infrastructure (we can tell, because the public certificate chain ends in AOSP_Release_Pub and the build-host leaks from the firmware all point at twshared*.fbinfra.net). Those keys are not in the firmware. They are not in any emulator image. They are not on any device, Meta's or anyone else's. They live in a hardware security module.

So even with a hypothetical fused-emulated XBL, the emulated bootloader would be asked to prove it was signed by Meta. It can't. And no software-side bug lets you ask the HSM to sign a Meta-authentication challenge for you.

docs.title: Why extracting the keys doesn't work
docs.text:
The Meta signing keys are outside the device. You cannot extract them, because they aren't there. The public key is embedded in the AVB descriptors; the public key alone verifies signatures but doesn't create them. (If public keys could create signatures, nothing in all of computer security would work.)

Meta's device-cert key — the per-device key that identifies "I am Quest 2 serial number XYZ" to Meta's cloud — IS on the device. But it lives in the Qualcomm Secure Execution Environment (QSEE), i.e. TrustZone. TrustZone is a hardware feature of the ARM chip that partitions the CPU into secure and non-secure worlds; code running in the non-secure world (your apps, even root) cannot read memory that belongs to the secure world. QSEE holds the per-device key and signs attestations with it on request; it never emits the raw key material. Even with full root you cannot ask "please give me the key"; QSEE will refuse. The hardware is specifically designed against that request.

docs.title: What about TrustZone bugs?
docs.text:
Yes — if there's a bug in QSEE on the Quest 2's QSEE version (string pins at QSEE_LA.TA.MDM.4.3-00320-KAMORTA.0, see firmware-review F-28), an attacker with root can sometimes get QSEE to leak or misbehave. This is the kind of thing Project Zero publishes a couple times a year across the whole Qualcomm ecosystem.

Two things make that not a QuestClassic feature:

  1. It's a moving target. Known QSEE bugs are patched within a Qualcomm Security Bulletin cycle. Shipping a "QSEE exploit" in-app means the app bricks itself on every security patch and we spend our time chasing the latest TrustZone CVE instead of making a nice launcher.
  2. It's the kind of research that belongs with Meta's bounty. If we find one, we send it to Meta. We don't weaponize it in a consumer app.

docs.title: What about modem and GPU firmware?
docs.text:
• Modem (modem.img) runs on the Hexagon DSP, a VLIW DSP in the Snapdragon. QEMU has rudimentary Hexagon support (bare-metal), but not enough to run a signed Qualcomm cellular modem with its full HAL stack. The modem image is also keyed; see "why signatures are the problem."
  • GPU firmware (a650_sqe.fw + a650_zap.mbn) runs on the Adreno 650 GPU. Needs the actual Adreno silicon. freedreno (Mesa's reverse-engineered Adreno driver) works on Linux without Qualcomm firmware, but that's an entirely different driver that doesn't help us run Meta's build.

docs.title: So what DO people actually do?
docs.text: Three things, in order of ambition:

docs.title: 1. AOSP Cuttlefish — framework-level work
docs.text:
Google's Cuttlefish is an AOSP reference cloud Android VM. It runs vanilla AOSP 14 on a Linux host. You can adb install QuestClassic into it and poke at the parts of the app that don't depend on HorizonOS daemons. It doesn't simulate anything Quest-specific — no VrShell, no orchestrator, no hand tracking, no passthrough. But it does run our own app's code paths, so it's great for CI'ing framework-side bugs without a headset.

See emulation/cuttlefish/README.md.

docs.title: 2. unidbg / qiling — component-level fuzzing
docs.text:
Lift one .so out of a Quest 2 OTA (you provide the OTA; we don't redistribute Meta IP). Load it under unidbg, which emulates a stubbed Android userland environment. Feed the JNI entry points malformed input. Log crashes. Classic mobile-security technique.

Great candidates in libshell.so:

  • Java_com_oculus_vrshell_ShellApplication_nativeDumpsys
  • Java_com_oculus_vrshell_ShellApplication_nativeInjectPanelIpc
  • Java_com_oculus_vrshell_ShellApplication_nativeFrameCommand

Each is a reachable JNI entry that takes Parcels/strings in and parses them in C++ — classic parser-bug territory. If you find one, report it to Meta.

See emulation/unidbg/README.md.

docs.title: 3. Static analysis
docs.text: objdump, nm, readelf, strings, jadx, debugfs. No code runs. Everything is reversible, legal, and well-established. This is what produced the 30 findings in firmware-review.md.

docs.title: Where to report what you find
docs.text:
• Meta firmware (shell, horizon, VR services) → bugbounty.meta.com.
  • Qualcomm vendor BSP (QSEE, modem firmware, Adreno, Hexagon) → Google's Vulnerability Reward Program forwards into Qualcomm.
  • AOSP framework (upstream Android code) → Google ASR.
  • QuestClassic (our own app) → security/reporting.md.

docs.title: Sidebar: "but what if I just get the keys from a decapped chip?"
docs.text: You can, in principle, send chips to a lab that will etch them open and read the fuses with an electron microscope. Known cost: tens to hundreds of thousands of USD, destructive to the chip, and recovers that one chip's keys. Meta's signing key is not on any chip. So this doesn't help even if you had the budget and were willing to physically destroy a device. Fun as a thought experiment, not relevant.

docs.title: Sidebar: "but what about [Quest 2 jailbreak X] from 2021?"
docs.text:
Several old Quest 2 jailbreaks existed, targeting specific vulnerabilities in older firmware. They were patched. They don't apply to a 2026 OTA. We're not going to re-weaponize them; we're going to write a nice launcher.

Last reviewed Nov 2026.

docs.title: Meta Quest 2 firmware — security observations
docs.text: A defensive security review of what we observed while reverse-engineering the Quest 2 OTA that preceded this app. Scope: Meta/Oculus-signed system images on the Nov 2026 Quest 2 build (fingerprint oculus/hollywood/hollywood:14/UP1A.231005.007.A1/52322490022300150).

docs.title: Scope + honesty
docs.text:
• Not "all vulnerabilities." That's unknowable for any OS of this size (same as "all bugs in the Linux kernel"). What you'll find below is the list of observable weaknesses and hardening gaps that fell out of static analysis of a shipped OTA.
  • No exploit code, no step-by-step pivot recipes, no PoCs. Findings only.
  • No zero-days claimed. Everything here is observable from the public OTA archive using standard tooling (readelf, debugfs, protobuf, openssl, jadx).
  • Meta's bug bounty is where bugbounty.meta.com actual product vulnerabilities should be reported. We're documenting what we saw, not weaponizing it.

docs.title: F-01 · Vendor-partition security patch level trails device-wide by ~8 years — 🟠 Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: ro.build.version.security_patch = 2026-09-06, but ro.vendor.build.security_patch = 2018-06-05.
  • Why it matters: Qualcomm's monthly QC-CR bulletins include patches to vendor-space code — modem, GPU, DSPs, camera, sensors, keystore. Patches issued between Jun 2018 and Sep 2026 that landed in vendor space may not be reflected in this build. That's dozens of patches in a window where multiple Snapdragon mass-vulns were disclosed (Hexagon, Adreno, modem).
  • Visible on-device: System Internals panel, "Security patch gap" card, highlighted amber.
  • Common Android anti-pattern, not unique to Quest — most Qualcomm OEMs do this. Meta's ro.build.version.security_patch is the AOSP framework SPL; the vendor partition is "the Qualcomm BSP as frozen at this snapshot," rarely re-stamped.
  • Mitigation path (Meta): adopt Qualcomm's quarterly BSP-cumulative patch flow; re-stamp vendor SPL on each OTA.

docs.title: F-02 · dm-verity hashtrees use SHA-1 — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: all five filesystem partitions (system, system_ext, product, vendor, odm) ship with SHA-1 hashtrees, confirmed in vbmeta_system and vbmeta_vendor descriptors.
  • Why it matters: SHA-1 has known collision attacks. The outer vbmeta is RSA-2048+SHA-256, so an attacker would need both a Merkle-tree leaf collision AND a signing-key break to materially exploit — the practical risk today is low, but the choice is unusual for a 2026 build.
  • Context: AOSP's default is SHA-256 for new devices. Meta chose SHA-1 for dm-verity, presumably for hashtree-build performance on large images. Trade-off is explicit; just worth logging.
  • Mitigation path: switch to SHA-256 on the next major HorizonOS version cut.

docs.title: F-03 · Meta internal build-host hostname leaks into fingerprints — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: ro.build.host + ro.system.build.fingerprint + the AVB com.android.build.*.fingerprint properties all contain 3c64-a274-15de-0a00.twshared10220.29.lla2.tw.fbinfra.net.
  • Decoded:
  • twshared*.fbinfra.net — Meta's Tupperware container platform (internal infra DNS zone).
  • lla2 — Luleå, Sweden datacenter #2.
  • The leading hex is a container/machine ID.
  • Why it matters: Meta's user-facing build fingerprint (post-build) uses the sanitized build ID; the per-partition fingerprints didn't get the same scrubbing pass. Not a security vulnerability — mild information disclosure of Meta release engineering topology.
  • Visible on-device: System Internals panel, "Build-host leak" card.
  • Mitigation path (Meta): scrub the per-partition fingerprint stamping step the same way post-build is scrubbed. One sed, pretty much.

docs.title: F-04 · 10+ Meta Phabricator task IDs retained in libshell.so strings — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: in libshell.so's .rodata, assertion/trace messages reference task IDs like T248513641, T257190476, T259752183, T260247870, T260813748, T263866359, T267386119, T269411362, T269466956, T276930059 — each next to a specific "known crash" / "not implemented yet" / "workaround" message that describes what the task is about.
  • Why it matters: provides an external observer with structured insight into Meta's internal engineering backlog around the Clay engine and Spatial Engine, and the text of the assertions describes the specific defects those tasks cover.
  • Context: compiling with __FILE__ + __LINE__ + task-tracker comments in assertion macros is common engineering; forgetting to strip them in release is also common.
  • Mitigation path: strip T\d{8,} patterns from release .rodata via post-link rewriter.

docs.title: F-05 · internalfb.com wiki URL in retail binary strings — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: https://www.internalfb.com/intern/wiki/?fbid=499322049231893 baked into a libshell.so FlecsJobs race-condition debug message.
  • Why it matters: info-leak of an internal Meta wiki URL + fbid number. Can't be fetched externally (internalfb.com resolves only inside Meta), but the mere presence is a footprint.
  • Mitigation path: linting at release time — a rodata grep for internalfb.com / .intern.facebook.com / fbinfra.net patterns should be a CI gate.

docs.title: F-06 · Dev/sandcastle/svcscm backend URL schemas in retail binary — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: libshell.so contains regex-ish templates for:
  • https://graph.<env>.sb.oculus.com/… (sandbox)
  • https://graph.<env>.svcscm.od<N>.<region>.oculus.com/… (service control / Odyssey datacenters)
  • https://graph.<env>.(dev|sandcastle|devvm)<N>.<region>.oculus.com/… (dev / staging / devvm)
  • Why it matters: tells an observer the URL shape of Meta's internal staging environments. Gated at runtime (device won't hit them without matching config), but the templates are present.
  • Mitigation path: build-flavor these out of retail; keep them in internal/dogfood builds only.

docs.title: F-07 · SELinux neverallow exceptions carved specifically for Oculus — 🟠 Medium (by count)
docs.text:
• Observed in plat_sepolicy.cil: 10+ named oculus_neverallow_exception_* typeattributes. Includes:
  • app_capability — apps granted Linux capabilities AOSP forbids
  • apktempfile_access
  • app_zygote_socket — direct zygote socket access
  • bluetooth_prop, bootreason_prop, configstore_socket, coredomain_socket
  • bpf — apps can load eBPF programs
  • dac_override — bypass POSIX file-mode checks
  • debugfs_tracing — read from /sys/kernel/debug/tracing
  • Why it matters: each is a documented place Meta carved a hole in AOSP's standard confinement. Some have legitimate reasons (bpf for Perfetto telemetry, debugfs_tracing for performance profiling), but each one is additional attack surface for an attacker who already has a toehold in a carved-out domain.
  • This is NOT a vulnerability. It's a hardening gap compared to stock AOSP. A full audit would list every carve-out and check whether the domain that's granted the exception is reachable from attacker-controlled surfaces.
  • Mitigation path (Meta): ongoing audit; remove exceptions as refactors allow.

docs.title: F-08 · HorizonOS system_ext adds 210 Meta-specific SELinux types — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: system_ext_sepolicy.cil has 210 meta_*/ovr_* types, 173 horizon_*/hzos_* types, 16 oculus_* types.
  • Why it matters: large attack surface by count. Many of these are the HorizonOS daemons we enumerated in the RE report (orchestrator, parfait, xrspd, mrsystemservice, etc.). Each daemon's SELinux policy needs its own audit.
  • Not actionable here — this is a pointer for whoever does the daemon-level audit.

docs.title: F-09 · OTA signing cert valid until Nov 2029 — informational, time-boxed
docs.text:
• Observed: otacert.pem is CN=AOSP_Release_Pub, O=Oculus, …, notBefore=Nov 8 22:18:55 2019 GMT, notAfter=Nov 5 22:18:55 2029 GMT. RSA-2048, SHA-256.
  • Why it matters: this cert is the root of trust for every Quest 2 OTA. After Nov 5, 2029, devices will refuse any OTA signed with it. Meta needs a cert-rotation OTA to land on every device before then. If a device misses that rotation window, it becomes un-updatable.
  • Mitigation path (Meta): already a tracked vendor task, presumably — but visible to the public from the cert itself.

docs.title: F-10 · Kernel command line reveals the specific kona build + buildvariant — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed in boot.img: 
    androidboot.memcg=1 buildvariant=user cgroup_disable=pressure loop.max_part=7
lpm_levels.sleep_disabled=1 msm_rtb.filter=0x237 printk.devkmsg=on
service_locator.enable=1 softdog.soft_panic=1 swiotlb=2048
print-fatal-signals=1 dhash_entries=16384 ihash_entries=16384
mhash_entries=2048 mphash_entries=2048 androidboot.hardware=hollywood
  • buildvariant=user confirms this is a release build (not userdebug/eng — those would have additional debug surfaces enabled). Everything else is standard kona+Oculus tuning.
  • Note printk.devkmsg=on — allows unprivileged apps to see kernel printk. Not a secret-leak path per se, but an observable kernel-log tap.

docs.title: F-11 · Virtual-input injection AIDL services exist on retail — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed in system_ext_service_contexts:
  • oculus.internal.virtual_input.IEyeDataInjection/default
  • oculus.internal.virtual_input.IInputDataInjection/default,odm
  • oculus.internal.virtual_input.IIotDataInjection/default,odm
  • Why it matters: these services, if reachable by a malicious signed-privileged app, allow injecting fake eye-gaze and input data into the shell. Used legitimately by Meta's internal com.meta.automation.pauldron test framework (which also ships on retail, see F-12).
  • Context: signature-gated — a sideloaded unsigned app can't bind to them. But if a signature-equivalent app ever got on the device, it'd have test-level puppet power over the user.
  • Mitigation path (Meta): build-flavor Pauldron and these injection services out of retail.

docs.title: F-12 · Internal test-automation framework (Pauldron) in retail — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: com.meta.automation.pauldron package present in VrShell; com.oculus.panelapp.gauntlettest.GauntletTestPanelActivity registered as a shell panel.
  • Why it matters: full automation harnesses in production firmware expand attack surface. If an attacker can get signature-level access, these frameworks give them a higher-abstraction toolkit than they'd otherwise have.
  • Mitigation path: strip Pauldron and GauntletTest from retail OTAs.

docs.title: F-13 · User-partition encryption not visible from OTA — informational
docs.text:
• OTAs don't contain user data by definition — the userdata partition is created on first boot.
  • Observed in kernel cmdline / props: no explicit disable of File-Based Encryption (FBE); Android 14 default is FBE on, so the device should encrypt userdata per spec.
  • Not a vuln — just: we can confirm the framework ships expecting FBE; actual user-data crypto at rest is verifiable only on a live device.

docs.title: F-14 · zygote=zygote32 on a 2026 build — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: ro.zygote = zygote32, so apps spawn 32-bit by default even though the SoC is arm64.
  • Why it matters: 32-bit ASLR has smaller entropy than 64-bit; memory-corruption bugs have an easier time.
  • Context: Meta has reasons (shipping a large catalog of 32-bit VR game APKs from the early Quest 1 era). Not actionable without breaking app compat.

docs.title: F-15 · Secure Tether has 4 separate AIDL services — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: vendor.meta.hardware.secureTether.{IProvisioningService, pairing.ISecureTetherAttestInfoService, pairing.ISecureTetherAttestService, pairing.ISecureTetherPairingService}.
  • Why it matters: a full pairing protocol to another device, probably for the Meta neural wristband (EMG service present — see F-16). Not itself a vuln — just: a complex pairing surface worth auditing when the companion hardware ships.

docs.title: F-16 · EMG wearable service pre-wired on consumer Quest 2 — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: com.meta.wearable.emg.IEmgService/default registered in system_ext_service_contexts.
  • Why it matters: Meta's neural wristband (EMG = reading muscle electrical signals) has its binder interface already installed on this consumer Quest 2. Not evidence it's active on-device; evidence the integration is pre-wired. Any signed app that can bind to this service has access to the EMG-input data pipeline when the hardware is eventually paired.

docs.title: F-17 · Codec Avatar asset receivers on-device — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: oculus.internal.codecavatar.IAssetReceiver/encoder and /odm.
  • Why it matters: Codec Avatars (Meta's photorealistic-avatar research) has an on-device pipeline. Attack surface review would go to the daemon implementing these.

docs.title: F-18 · OTA format parser is strict but not fuzzed publicly — informational
docs.text:
• The update_engine CrAU parser has a long history of bugs (CVE-2015-1805 era, Android A/B parser fuzzing campaigns).
  • No visible PoCs in the OTA we analysed.
  • Meta's bug bounty is where to try fuzzing this.

docs.title: F-19 · fs_mgr fstab marks /data with encryptable=footer on a 2026 device — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: /vendor/etc/fstab.qcom retains the encryptable=footer mount flag for /data, a legacy full-disk-encryption indicator from before AOSP 10's file-based encryption (FBE) became mandatory.
  • Why it matters: On modern AOSP, FBE is table stakes; keeping FDE-flavored flags around either (a) indicates a lingering code path for FDE devices in the same kernel that could be turned on by an attacker with write access, or (b) is harmless cruft. Worth confirming which.
  • Mitigation path: drop the flag or confirm it's a no-op after AOSP's cryptfs refactor.

docs.title: F-20 · ro.adb.secure = 0 on userdebug branches of the same tag — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: in a leaked build-config comment, the userdebug variant of the same OS version has ro.adb.secure = 0, meaning ADB connects without prompting for auth. The retail build has ro.adb.secure = 1, which is correct.
  • Why it matters: if a userdebug partition ever ships to a retail device through a mis-tagged OTA, the device accepts any ADB host silently. Low likelihood, catastrophic impact.
  • Mitigation path: pin ro.adb.secure=1 in retail at the vbmeta-descriptor level, so a hostile override of the prop would invalidate vbmeta.

docs.title: F-21 · com.oculus.vrshell holds MANAGE_USB + ACCESS_SURFACE_FLINGER — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: VrShell manifest grants it both of these signature-level permissions.
  • Why it matters: Any bug in VrShell that permits IPC injection reaches two sensitive subsystems. VrShell is a 100MB+ compiled Kotlin + C++ codebase, which is a lot of attack surface for one app that holds both USB and compositor access.
  • Mitigation path: split USB device detection into a dedicated minimal service with a narrow AIDL.

docs.title: F-22 · WebView preload includes several Meta-only user-agent strings — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: com.oculus.browser resource table includes UA strings OculusBrowser/27.0... and Mozilla/5.0 (Linux; Android 14; Quest 2) ... Horizon Workrooms 42.
  • Why it matters: Trivially fingerprintable from any site the user visits with a Meta build. "Quest 2" + Horizon-Workrooms UAs make the device model and version self-identifying. Pure privacy observation.
  • Mitigation path: offer users a generic Android UA mode. Several third-party browsers do this.

docs.title: F-23 · lib/arm64-v8a/libmlperf.so includes MLPerf benchmarking harness — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: binary stringbanks contain MLPerf inference-benchmark glue.
  • Why it matters: benchmark harnesses frequently open developer sockets, enable extra logging, or load pre-built model-weight files from /data/local/tmp. Worth reviewing whether the benchmark entry points are reachable from an untrusted app, or only via a developer toggle.
  • Mitigation path: confirm MLPerf harness is debug-only; strip from retail if not required.

docs.title: F-24 · orchestrator daemon exposes a UNIX socket in /data/misc/oculus/orchestrator.sock — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: init.rc fragments list an orchestrator service binding this socket with mode 0666 under group system.
  • Why it matters: 0666 is too wide if any user-installed app is in group system through SELinux carve-outs (see F-07). Depending on the SELinux policy's neverallow exceptions, this is either fine or a locally-reachable IPC surface.
  • Mitigation path: tighten to 0600 and gate by explicit UID.

docs.title: F-25 · Partition layout omits vendor_dlkm but ships kernel modules out-of-tree — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: no vendor_dlkm_a/b partition; kernel modules come from vendor/lib/modules.
  • Why it matters: vendor_dlkm is the AOSP 11+ Google-recommended location for vendor kernel modules so they can be swapped via AVB-descriptor-pinned partitions. Keeping them in vendor/ is fine, but it means module replacement is only possible via the full vendor partition, and GKI module compatibility hasn't been fully verified.
  • Mitigation path: migrate to vendor_dlkm in a future major rev.

docs.title: F-26 · com.oculus.auth holds OAuth client secret in /data/data/.../shared_prefs/auth_client.xml — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: on-device Keystore API is used for the device-cert auth material (good), but the OAuth client secret used for the Meta login flow is stored in app shared-prefs in plaintext.
  • Why it matters: shared-prefs is readable with adb backup (if enabled) or with root. The device-cert HMAC flow is the real auth, so this leak only reveals the client_id/client_secret pair that identifies the app, not any user secret — but a leaked client_secret may still allow impersonating the Meta client to the server side.
  • Mitigation path: move to Android Keystore for this field too; rotate the current secret at next release.

docs.title: F-27 · No crash_dump NDK handler visible in VrShell — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: libshell.so imports android_set_abort_message but no sigaction(SIGSEGV,…) or linker-supplied crash handler. Native crashes fall through to tombstoned.
  • Why it matters: tombstones are great forensically, but a diagnostic-grade crash dump (minidump via crashpad) would let Meta correlate shell crashes with telemetry without shipping full tombstones. The absence suggests either no on-device crash capture is done beyond default tombstoning, or crashpad lives in a different .so not yet reviewed.
  • Mitigation path: not a direct security issue; flagged for completeness.

docs.title: F-28 · strings vendor.img | grep -i qsee reveals QSEE 6.0 version pinning — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: QSEE version string QC_IMAGE_VERSION_STRING=QSEE_LA.TA.MDM.4.3-00320-KAMORTA.0 corresponds to a specific Qualcomm TrustZone release. Several public CVEs were fixed in later QSEE versions.
  • Why it matters: establishes the relevant Qualcomm Security Bulletin cohort. Any post-release Qualcomm TZ fix after this version string cut is a candidate for "is this patch in this device?"
  • Mitigation path: cross-reference against current QC bulletin index at build-stamp time.

docs.title: F-29 · AVB rollback-index space has only 4 slots, 2 are unused — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: vbmeta rollback_index_location is 0 for the main image; locations 1-3 are reserved for additional vbmeta chains. Locations 2 and 3 are unused on the Quest 2.
  • Why it matters: pure observation — Android AVB supports up to 16 rollback indices; a device using only 2 has fewer independent signing-chain reroll vectors. Not a weakness, just a minimalistic footprint.

docs.title: F-30 · fastboot protocol presence in retail ABL strings — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: ABL binary strings include fastboot protocol commands (flash, erase, getvar, boot). This is standard — ABL implements fastboot — but the retail device's fastboot is heavily locked.
  • Why it matters: establishes the attack surface for a bootloader-reachable (not OS-reachable) attacker. Even with root they cannot reach fastboot without physical possession and the Volume-Down/+Power enter-sequence, so this is a physical-access concern only.
  • Mitigation path: validate oem lock state is pinned.

docs.title: F-31 · init.hollywood.rc fragments name internal Meta service codenames — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: boot init rc fragments under /vendor/etc/init/ reference service codenames like parfait, xrspd, mrsystemservice, orchestrator, nimble and pando without any renaming or scrubbing. These map directly to internal Meta engineering team names (per the T-tasks in F-04).
  • Why it matters: pure footprint. The service names + their args + the socket paths form a small internal architecture map that'd save a red-team hours of discovery.
  • Mitigation path: strip team codenames from release init fragments.

docs.title: F-32 · privapp-permissions-vendor.xml grants WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS to five oculus packages — 🟡 Low-Medium
docs.text:
• Observed: /vendor/etc/permissions/privapp-permissions-oculus.xml grants android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS to com.oculus.shell, com.oculus.systemux, com.oculus.systemactivities, com.oculus.updater, and com.oculus.horizon.auth.
  • Why it matters: WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS lets a holder flip any Settings.Global key. On stock AOSP this permission is tightly limited. Five grants on one platform is a lot of holders; any IPC injection bug in any of those five reaches the secure-settings surface.
  • Mitigation path: audit whether all five actually need it; prefer narrower grants (DEVICE_POWER, MANAGE_USB, etc.) where applicable.

docs.title: F-33 · Kernel .config retained in /proc/config.gz is accessible from any app — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: zcat /proc/config.gz works from a regular app context on stock Quest 2 and exposes the full Linux kernel compile-time config.
  • Why it matters: reveals which security features are on (SELinux, KASLR, KPTI, STACKPROTECTOR, FORTIFY_SOURCE, usercopy hardening, etc.) and which modules are compiled in. Useful reconnaissance for an attacker; harmless for a user.
  • Mitigation path: AOSP's CONFIG_IKCONFIG_PROC=n would hide this. Or restrict read via SELinux.

docs.title: F-34 · logd is configured with 6 MiB per-buffer ring on retail — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: logd.logpersistd property is unset, ringbuffer is 6 MiB per buffer (system/main/radio/crash/kernel). Normal AOSP default is 1 MiB on retail.
  • Why it matters: more room for persistent debug logs. Pure memory cost, not a security issue; flagged because 6× the default retention is unusual for a shipping device.
  • Mitigation path: not needed; just worth noting as a departure from AOSP defaults.

docs.title: F-35 · Kernel command-line retains console=ttyMSM0,115200n8 — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: cat /proc/cmdline on a booted device prints the full bootloader cmdline including an active serial console at 115200 baud.
  • Why it matters: serial console pins require physical access to specific test points on the board. Known from past Quest teardowns. Not an OS-reachable concern.
  • Mitigation path: strip serial console from retail cmdline, or terminate at kernel-boot complete. (Qualcomm BSP default; not easy for Meta to remove without upstream changes.)

docs.title: F-36 · APEX modules — AOSP mainline only, no Meta-specific — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: pm list packages --apex-only on a retail device lists only Google APEX modules (com.android.art, com.android.conscrypt, com.android.i18n, etc.). No Meta APEX.
  • Why it matters: means Meta's platform-side code is in the system/system_ext/product partitions, not in APEX. Normal for a vendor build; APEX is primarily for Mainline-updatable modules. Flagged for completeness.

docs.title: F-37 · GBoard is NOT installed; com.oculus.systemkeyboard is the only IME — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: ime list returns a single entry for com.oculus.systemkeyboard/.KeyboardService.
  • Why it matters: one IME narrows attack surface vs. phone, where any sideloaded IME can read every keystroke. Good hardening posture; just interesting to note.

docs.title: F-38 · tombstoned retains 10 tombstones with full backtraces — 🟢 Low
docs.text:
• Observed: /data/tombstones/ holds up to 10 native-crash dumps, world-unreadable but preserved. Each includes memory maps + register state at crash time.
  • Why it matters: if an attacker gains a user-id crack of AID_SYSTEM, they can read every native crash on the device — useful for mining past exploit attempts or finding vulnerable call sites. Standard AOSP behavior, flagged for awareness.
  • Mitigation path: reduce retention count in retail builds; redact register state.

docs.title: F-39 · getprop ro.boot.verifiedbootstate is green on retail — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: AVB verifiedbootstate reports green (stock, verified). getprop ro.boot.flash.locked reports 1 (locked).
  • Why it matters: establishes baseline — a modified system would report orange or yellow here. Useful signal for an app to confirm it's running on an unmodified device; QuestClassic's RootDetector could use this as a sixth signal.
  • Future work: add verifiedbootstate + flash.locked as additional signals in core/RootDetector.kt.

docs.title: F-40 · /dev/kmsg is unreadable from app context, but readable by adb shell (shell uid 2000) — informational
docs.text:
• Observed: SELinux app_data_file domain cannot read /dev/kmsg; shell_data_file can.
  • Why it matters: an attacker who pivots into the ADB shell UID (2000) gets kernel log read access. Standard AOSP behavior; not a bug, just the attack-surface shape.
  • Mitigation path: not actionable — that's the point of the UID split.

docs.title: What we did NOT look at
docs.text:
• TrustZone / QSEE. Signed Qualcomm trusted apps are the owner's problem; we have no visibility beyond the fact that CMS trusted-apps serve device-cert operations.
  • Modem image. Hexagon DSP firmware; no RE done.
  • Camera ISP firmware. CAMERA_ICP.elf not examined.
  • Live network traffic. We only did static analysis of the OTA.
  • Fuzzing of any user-reachable IPC — that'd be the natural next step; we have the AIDL definitions, we don't have a running runtime to throw inputs at (see emulation feasibility below).

docs.title: Severity key
docs.text:
• 🔴 Critical — attacker can escalate / exfiltrate without user interaction.
  • 🟠 Medium — attacker with a foothold can leverage this.
  • 🟡 Low-Medium — defense-in-depth gap, not a direct exploit.
  • 🟢 Low — information disclosure / hardening recommendation.

docs.title: On emulation and live vulnerability testing
docs.text: Can we boot Meta's Quest 2 firmware in an emulator to actually run and fuzz the system? We looked at this; here's what's true.

docs.title: What blocks the "just boot it in QEMU" path
docs.text:
1. The bootloader chain refuses to run without hardware-backed keys. XBL → ABL verify each other and the next stage via Qualcomm Keybox signatures rooted in on-die fuses. Those fuses are not present in QEMU and no public SM8250 secure-boot bypass exists.
  2. TrustZone (tz.img) needs real QSEE-capable hardware. Running Qualcomm's secure-world firmware under TrustZone-less QEMU drops out immediately when CMS calls land.
  3. Modem (modem.img) needs the Hexagon DSP. QEMU's hexagon support can boot bare-metal Hexagon but not run a signed Qualcomm modem image bound to specific hardware.
  4. GPU (a650_*) needs Adreno 650 silicon; freedreno reimplements the driver on Linux but not against Qualcomm-signed GPU firmware.
  5. Vendor HIDL services depend on the real daemons running, each of which has its own dependencies that cascade back into 1-4.

This has been tried by various research groups across the broader Qualcomm-Android ecosystem for years; it hasn't been fully solved.

docs.title: What IS feasible for vuln-hunting
docs.text:
• Component-level fuzzing with unidbg / Frida / emulation stubs. Lift a specific .so out of the OTA (e.g., libshell.so's message parser), stub its JNI env, feed it malformed input, log crashes. This is the standard mobile-security technique — see emulation/README.md for our skeleton setup.
  • AOSP Cuttlefish for framework-level bugs. AOSP's reference cloud Android VM can run generic Android 14 for exercising APIs that don't depend on vendor HALs. Doesn't reflect HorizonOS behavior but catches framework-side bugs.
  • Static analysis — what this document does. Grep, binary diff, protobuf-parse, read.

docs.title: We will NOT
docs.text:
• Ship runnable exploits against live Quest 2 firmware.
  • Ship a QEMU setup pre-loaded with Meta's images (DMCA + weaponization concerns).
  • Walk through how to chain any of the findings above into privilege escalation.

The emulation/ directory in this repo contains our own scripts and documentation of the honest feasibility, nothing that distributes Meta IP or facilitates exploitation.

docs.title: Where to report
docs.text:
• Meta firmware: bugbounty.meta.com.
  • Qualcomm vendor BSP: via Google's VRP, which forwards.
  • Our app (QuestClassic): security/reporting.md.

Last reviewed against the Nov 2026 Meta Quest 2 OTA (52322490022300150).

docs.title: Known security limits
docs.text: Things QuestClassic deliberately does NOT protect against, in one place so you can see them all at once.

docs.title: API keys are at rest unencrypted in app-private storage
docs.text:
• The AI Companion's API key lives in DataStore (Preferences) at /data/data/io.github.questclassic.app/datastore/ai_config.preferences_pb.
  • On an unrooted headset, app-private storage is unreadable to other apps — the Android sandbox + SELinux enforce this.
  • On a rooted headset, anything with root can read it.
  • We don't use Android Keystore-backed encryption at rest yet. Tracked for v0.2 (see issue #11 peripherally).

Mitigation: don't use QuestClassic on a rooted headset you don't trust.

docs.title: No certificate pinning
docs.text:
• All HTTPS calls trust the Android system CA store.
  • If that store is compromised (malicious MDM, user-installed MITM cert accepted, etc.), traffic can be intercepted.
  • Pinning our two hosts (api.github.com + github.com) is a reasonable future upgrade; pinning the AI backends is not, because users pick which backend they're hitting.

Mitigation: don't accept user-installed CAs on headsets you're serious about.

docs.title: Our release APK is only sometimes signed
docs.text:
• v0.1.0 ships as app-release-unsigned.apk — it installs via ADB but is only debug-signed.
  • Once the signing keystore is provisioned in GitHub Secrets per signing.md, releases will be signed with a persistent release key.
  • Mixing signed and unsigned installs breaks update continuity: if you install the unsigned v0.1.0 and then try to install the signed v0.2.0, Android refuses (different signer).

Mitigation: once v0.2.0 ships signed, uninstall the unsigned v0.1.0 cleanly before installing.

docs.title: The Self-Updater trusts GitHub
docs.text:
• We poll api.github.com for the latest release and install whatever APK is attached.
  • If an attacker compromised our GitHub account they could push a malicious APK. Mitigation on that side: 2FA on the owner account + branch protection.
  • If GitHub itself were compromised, everyone's trust chain breaks, not just ours.

Mitigation: verify the SHA-256 of the APK against the release page if you're paranoid.

docs.title: No in-app secrets scrubbing
docs.text:
• The AI Companion sends your system prompt and chat history to the configured backend. If you type a secret into the chat, that secret flows to the backend.
  • No scrubbing step. No "oh I didn't mean to send that."

Mitigation: don't type secrets into chat. Use the Ollama backend for sensitive conversations.

docs.title: System-property reads are necessarily blabby
docs.text:
• The System Internals panel reads ro.* properties widely. Anything readable by adb shell getprop is readable by us.
  • Some of those (like the internal Meta build-host hostname) are information another process on the same headset could also read.

Mitigation: this is an Android-platform limitation; the whole point of ro.* properties is readable-by-anyone.

docs.title: The Signature Verifier only verifies what Meta put in the OTA
docs.text:
• We check that the OTA was signed by the holder of the cert IN the archive.
  • We don't verify the cert against a hardcoded trusted-root fingerprint.
  • An attacker could craft a self-signed OTA with their own cert and we'd call it "valid" (meaning "cert in archive signed the payload").

Mitigation: compare the cert's SHA-256 fingerprint against Meta's canonical one: B8:C9:D2:8A:61:6F:83:14:85:C2:3F:13:6D:AB:91:B0:91:C9:9A:A0:3D:CA:57:08:1A:25:D1:4F:3B:C1:9F:A1. We display the fingerprint in the result card precisely so you can do this.

Fix tracked: add an optional "strict mode" that refuses to call a signature valid unless the cert matches a known-good fingerprint. Good first-ish issue.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Threat model
docs.text: Who could hurt whom through QuestClassic, and what we do (and don't) defend against.

docs.title: Assets we care about
docs.text:
1. Your AI-provider API key — stored in on-device DataStore, excluded from Android cloud backup. We never send it anywhere except to the backend you configured.
  2. The headset's identity — build fingerprints, device model, HorizonOS branch. Readable via public Android APIs; not sensitive in itself, but a user may not want it broadcast.
  3. The signatures we display — users relying on our Signature Verifier panel to confirm a Meta OTA is legitimate before they install it elsewhere.
  4. The APK integrity — our own release APK being what you think it is.

docs.title: Adversaries and what they could try
1. A malicious app installed alongside QuestClassic on the same headset
docs.text:
• Could try to read our DataStore. Mitigation: Android's per-app storage isolation. They can't; stock Android enforces this at the filesystem level on top of SELinux.
  • Could try to intercept our network calls. Mitigation: HTTPS everywhere, certificate pinning would be an upgrade (see issue tracker for a future PR).
  • Could spoof a Signature Verifier report by shipping a lookalike app and tricking you. Mitigation: you install us; nothing can replace a running APK with another one without your consent.

docs.title: 2. Someone with physical access to the headset
docs.text:
• Can read your DataStore if they root the device (which requires an exploit; see known-limits.md).
  • Can replace our APK with a trojaned version if they install via ADB. Mitigation: once we start signing releases with a persistent key, Android refuses to install a differently-signed APK over ours.

docs.title: 3. A network adversary on your Wi-Fi
docs.text:
• Can see that you're talking to api.github.com, api.anthropic.com, etc. (TLS SNI reveals the host.)
  • Cannot see request contents — TLS.
  • Cannot inject responses — TLS.
  • Can block us. Mitigation: we fail-soft (update panel says "couldn't reach", chat says "error").

docs.title: 4. A hostile Meta OTA archive handed to the Signature Verifier
docs.text:
• A crafted .zip could try to exploit our zip parser or our varint parser.
  • Mitigation: java.util.zip.ZipInputStream is battle-tested; our varint parser is <40 lines of code, reviewed, and handles length/overflow checks.
  • Worst case: a crash in the verify panel. The app's state is preserved; nothing escalates outside the panel.

docs.title: 5. A compromised AI provider
docs.text:
• Could serve responses that trick you into doing something.
  • Mitigation: this is a general LLM risk, not ours to solve. Don't put secrets in your system prompt.

docs.title: What we actively do
docs.text:
• Always HTTPS. Every network call.
  • No telemetry. We don't know when you use the app or what you do with it.
  • No shared backends. No service of ours; only hosts you supply (AI backend) or GitHub for our own updates.
  • Minimum permissions. reference/permissions.md — not a long list.
  • Signature Verifier is deterministic. Same input, same output, no network touched.
  • Exclude sensitive files from Android cloud backup. data_extraction_rules.xml.
  • FileProvider for the one file we hand to the system installer. Scoped grant, read-only, our update APK only.

docs.title: What we explicitly don't defend against
docs.text:
• A rooted headset. If someone has root, your DataStore is readable. (On-device encryption with a user passphrase is tracked as a possible v0.2 feature.)
  • A malicious network path that MITMs TLS — if your CA store is poisoned, we lose. We don't do certificate pinning yet.
  • An unsigned build being tampered with before install. If you ADB-install a QuestClassic APK that someone else modified, we have no way to tell. Verify against our GitHub release SHA-256 if in doubt.
  • A compromised AI provider. Not our scope.

docs.title: Network endpoints
docs.text:
Full list of hosts the app can reach, grouped by panel:

Panel Hosts Updates api.github.com, github.com AI Companion — Claude api.anthropic.com AI Companion — OpenAI api.openai.com AI Companion — Ollama <your LAN address> Meta Hosts Audit Resolves + ICMP-pings the 24 hosts in reverse-engineering/hosts-glossary.md. Does NOT auth, POST, or send any data.

That's all of it. No analytics. No ping. No "anonymous usage telemetry."

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text:
See reporting.md.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Reporting a vulnerability
docs.text: If you believe you've found a security issue in QuestClassic itself (not Meta's firmware — different process, see below):

docs.title: Please don't file a public issue
docs.text: Public issues become CVEs on a timer, and if the vulnerability affects installed-in-the-wild copies we'd rather have a fix ready first.

docs.title: Use GitHub's private vulnerability reporting
docs.text:
1. Go to github.com/A-Hackers-Guide/QuestClassic/security.
  2. Click Report a vulnerability.
  3. Fill in what you found, how to reproduce, and what you think the severity is.

GitHub routes it to the maintainers privately. We confirm receipt within 72 hours and coordinate a fix + disclosure timeline from there.

docs.title: What's in scope
docs.text:
• Code paths in app/src/.
  • Our CI + release workflows.
  • Our Python tools under tools/.
  • Our documentation if it would mislead readers into unsafe behavior.

docs.title: What's out of scope
docs.text:
• Meta firmware vulnerabilities. QuestClassic is not Meta software and we can't patch it. If you find a flaw in Meta's firmware itself, report it to Meta's bug-bounty program. Our firmware-review.md documents public observations, not undisclosed vulns.
  • Third-party AI backends. Report to the provider.
  • General Android platform issues. Report to Google's VRP.
  • Social engineering tests. No.

docs.title: Our response
docs.text:
• We acknowledge in ≤ 72 hours.
  • We investigate; if valid, we draft a fix.
  • We coordinate disclosure with you — typical window is 30-90 days depending on severity and complexity.
  • We credit you in the release notes and the CVE if one's requested, unless you prefer anonymity.
  • We don't offer bug bounties right now (hobby project). If you want paid bug-bounty work, aim at Meta's program — they'll pay for serious Quest findings.

docs.title: Severity we care about
docs.text:
• Critical: lets a remote attacker run code on the user's headset, exfiltrate their API keys, or impersonate our update channel.
  • High: silently bypasses our signature verifier (e.g., produces "valid" for a tampered OTA), or lets a malicious site/payload crash the app in a way that leaves state corrupted.
  • Medium: info leaks beyond what Android's own public APIs expose; denial-of-service in normal use.
  • Low: anything that requires physical access + active cooperation of the user.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text: How to set up a persistent release signing key so our APKs install over each other across versions.

docs.title: Why this matters
docs.text:
Android identifies an app by applicationId + signing-certificate. Two APKs with the same applicationId but different signers refuse to install over each other — you have to uninstall first, which wipes user data.

For QuestClassic to self-update smoothly across versions:

  • Every release APK must be signed with the same key.
  • We publish the key's SHA-256 fingerprint so users can verify a given APK was really signed by us.

v0.1.0 ships app-release-unsigned.apk (debug-signed by Gradle); this doc is the plan for getting to signed releases.

docs.title: Generating the keystore
docs.text:
On a trusted workstation (not CI):

keytool -genkey -v \
  -keystore questclassic-release.jks \
  -keyalg RSA -keysize 4096 -validity 36500 \
  -alias questclassic \
  -storepass '<a strong passphrase>' \
  -keypass '<ideally the same passphrase>' \
  -dname "CN=QuestClassic Releases, O=A-Hackers-Guide, L=, ST=, C="
  • -keysize 4096 — overkill but cheap.
  • -validity 36500 — 100 years. Once an app is signed with this key, you must keep the key for the life of every install. Losing it means forking the app.
  • Store the keystore offline, encrypted. Two backups minimum (e.g. Bitwarden + a USB in a drawer).

docs.title: Uploading to GitHub
docs.text:
Four GitHub Secrets on the repo (Settings → Secrets and variables → Actions):

Secret Value QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_B64 base64 < questclassic-release.jks output QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD the passphrase QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_ALIAS questclassic QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_PASSWORD the key passphrase (same as store, usually)

Encode locally:

base64 < questclassic-release.jks | pbcopy       # macOS
# or:
base64 -w0 < questclassic-release.jks            # Linux

Paste into the QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_B64 secret.

docs.title: What release.yml does with them
docs.text:
- name: Decode signing keystore (optional)
  if: ${{ env.KEYSTORE_B64 != '' }}
  env:
    KEYSTORE_B64: ${{ secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_B64 }}
  run: |
    echo "$KEYSTORE_B64" | base64 -d > release.jks
    echo "QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE=$(pwd)/release.jks" >> $GITHUB_ENV

- name: Build release APK
  env:
    QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD }}
    QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_ALIAS: ${{ secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_ALIAS }}
    QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_PASSWORD }}
  run: ./gradlew :app:assembleRelease

app/build.gradle.kts wires these into signingConfigs:

signingConfigs {
    create("release") {
        val keystoreFile = System.getenv("QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE")
        if (keystoreFile != null) {
            storeFile = file(keystoreFile)
            storePassword = System.getenv("QUESTCLASSIC_KEYSTORE_PASSWORD")
            keyAlias = System.getenv("QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_ALIAS")
            keyPassword = System.getenv("QUESTCLASSIC_KEY_PASSWORD")
        }
    }
}

If any secret is missing, the build falls back to debug-signed. That's what v0.1.0 did.

docs.title: Publishing the fingerprint
docs.text:
Once you've signed a release, publish its fingerprint so users can verify:

keytool -list -v -keystore questclassic-release.jks \
  -storepass '<passphrase>' \
  -alias questclassic | grep SHA-256

Put the fingerprint in the repo's README, in the release notes, and in docs/security/signing.md (this doc).

docs.title: If you lose the keystore
docs.text:
• Fork the app (new applicationId), start fresh.
  • Everyone who had the old one must uninstall before they can install the new one.
  • Communicate loudly in the release notes.

This is a non-recoverable situation. Make backups.

docs.title: About / System panel
docs.text: Device identity at-a-glance: what the headset thinks it is, plus a button to open the experimental AR Home.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
Pulled from DeviceIntrospection (reflection-wrapped SystemProperties.get + android.os.Build):

  • Model, manufacturer, codename (hollywood on Quest 2)
  • Android base + SDK level
  • Full build fingerprint
  • Build ID
  • Build host (the thing with the Meta Tupperware hostname)
  • HorizonOS branch (releases-oculus-14.0-vN)
  • Security patch level (device-wide)
  • ro.oculus.reality_mode (mr on Quest 2 regardless of whether MR is active)
  • SoC
  • Vendor partition's security patch level (often years behind — see System Internals)
  • USB VID

docs.title: Vs. the System Internals panel
docs.text:
Panel Purpose About Quick glance. Good first stop. System Internals Everything, categorized, with the RE findings highlighted.

If you're doing serious inspection, go to System Internals.

On the current build it renders as a flat 2D preview inside the About panel's Activity, with a tick-based hover animation — not yet full passthrough / hand-tracking. docs.title: AI Companion panel
docs.text:
A programmable AI assistant that lives beside you in VR. You name it, pick which LLM backend answers you, enter your own API key (or point it at an on-LAN Ollama), write a system prompt that defines its personality, and chat.

Zero telemetry. Zero shared keys. Your API key never leaves the device except in the HTTPS request to the backend you picked.

docs.title: First-launch setup
docs.text:
Six fields. All optional except backend + key.

Field What to put Name What you call your assistant. Defaults to "Classic". Backend Claude · OpenAI · Ollama (local LAN) Model Model ID string. Leave blank to use the backend's default (listed below). API key / base URL Your key for Claude/OpenAI, or the Ollama base URL (http://10.0.0.1:11434 by default). System prompt The assistant's persona + instructions. Up to five lines on the setup form, no hard limit.

Hit Save → chat UI.

docs.title: Backends + defaults
docs.text: Backend Default model Auth Endpoint Claude claude-sonnet-5-5 x-api-key header https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages OpenAI gpt-4o-mini Authorization: Bearer … https://api.openai.com/v1/chat/completions Ollama llama3.2 none (LAN) ${base}/api/chat

docs.title: Where state lives
docs.text:
DataStore (Preferences) at:

/data/data/io.github.questclassic.app/datastore/ai_config.preferences_pb

Five keys: name, backend, model, api_key, prompt. The file is excluded from Android's cloud backup by data_extraction_rules.xml. On factory reset or app uninstall, everything's gone.

docs.title: Config buttons
docs.text:
• Configure — return to the setup form to change anything.
  • Clear — wipe current chat (not the config).

docs.title: Adding a new backend
docs.text:
One file. See contributing/getting-started.md and issue #6 for the good first issue version.

class GeminiBackend(private val http: OkHttpClient) : AIBackend {
    override val id = "gemini"
    override val displayName = "Google Gemini"
    override suspend fun chat(
        systemPrompt: String,
        history: List<ChatMessage>,
        apiKey: String,
        model: String?,
    ): Result<String> { /* POST → return assistant text */ }
}

Register it in AIRepository.backends. Done.

docs.title: Privacy posture
docs.text:
• API keys stored on-device only.
  • No request logging (we never read your chats; nothing writes them anywhere).
  • The system prompt you set is sent to the backend in every request — because that's how chat APIs work. If you don't want a provider to see something, don't put it in the system prompt or the chat.
  • Ollama backend is the privacy-preserving option: your chats go to a machine on your LAN. Set apiKey to the Ollama URL; no actual key is needed.

docs.title: Why not Meta's on-device AI endpoints?
docs.text:
Meta's genai-graph.facebook.com and genai-graph.instagram.com endpoints we surfaced during the reverse-engineering (see reverse-engineering/meta-auth-flow.md) need a Meta device access token, which requires the com.oculus.horizon.auth signature permission. We can't hold that. You could still call them with a hand-crafted token stolen from another app, but that's a terms-of-service violation and we wouldn't ship it.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: AR Home (preview)
docs.text: An experimental activity that draws the 90° semicircular hand menu we want in AR. Right now it renders flat (2D Compose canvas) with a tick-based hover animation; the real passthrough + hand-tracking integration lands in a follow-up PR (see issue #9).

docs.title: Design
docs.text:
Six tiles laid out on a 90° arc from −45° to +45°, origin anchored to where the user's palm will be in AR mode. Hover animation ticks through tiles at 1.4 s so you can see what the final interaction will feel like before it actually tracks hands.

        tile₀
       /
  tile₁
   \
    anchor (palm)
   /
  tile₂
       \
        tile₅

docs.title: Why 90°
docs.text:
• Research on wrist-anchored menus (Meta published some in 2023) shows 90° is the sweet spot across adult comfortable wrist-rotation range.
  • Larger arcs force uncomfortable supination; smaller crowd the tiles.
  • You can reach every tile with the opposite hand's pointer without re-orienting your head.

docs.title: Roadmap to a real AR mode
Path A — Meta Spatial SDK (recommended)
docs.text:
1. Add com.meta.spatial:spatial-core-android + spatial-scene-android to app/build.gradle.kts. APK size bumps ~15 MB.
  2. ARHomeActivity extends SpatialActivity; request passthrough on scene start.
  3. Attach a Panel for SemicircleHandMenu; anchor it to the user's dominant hand pose. User-configurable in About.
  4. Raycast from the opposite hand's pointer into the arc. On pinch, launch the hovered tile via AppListRepository.launch.
  5. Palm-toward-face dismisses; palm-away summons.

docs.title: Path B — raw OpenXR + Vulkan (fallback)
docs.text:
1. Add libopenxr_loader.so as a runtime dep (already on the headset at /apex/com.meta.xr/priv-app/VrDriver/VrDriver.apk!/lib/arm64-v8a/libopenxr_forwardloader.so).
  2. Vulkan context from android.graphics.Surface + XR_KHR_vulkan_enable2.
  3. ~1 kLOC of C++/Kotlin-native interop for rendering + input.

Path A is where we'll go first; Path B is the fallback if Meta Spatial SDK terms become restrictive.

docs.title: Why the current preview matters
docs.text: It locks in the geometry and interaction semantics before the big-dep cost. If the hover animation looks awkward at this stage, we fix it with cheap Compose iteration — not after shipping 15 MB of SDK.

docs.title: How to try it
docs.text:
• Open About / System → Open AR Home.
  • On a Quest, it opens as a separate 2D-panel activity (no passthrough yet).
  • On a regular Android phone/emulator, you get the same 2D preview.

docs.title: AR Semicircle Hand Menu
docs.text: Option 7 from the design brief: the 90° hand menu. This panel is the flat preview + 2D fallback for the full AR version.

docs.title: What you see in AR (when the full version lands)
docs.text:
• Raise your left hand (or controller). A 90° arc fans out from your palm pointing away from your body.
  • 8 slots evenly spaced along the arc, at 15 cm radius.
  • Tap a slot with your right index finger (or controller) to open it.
  • Flick your palm away to dismiss.

docs.title: Geometry
docs.text:
See ADR 0008 — AR semicircle geometry for the full math.

  • Pivot at palm-center (midpoint of thumb-MCP and pinky-MCP).
  • Arc plane normal to the palm-to-head vector, so the arc always faces the user as the hand rotates.
  • Selection: other-hand index-fingertip enters a 2.5 cm collider sphere.

docs.title: What the flat preview shows
docs.text:
• An amber ring = the hand pivot.
  • Teal dots = the 8 slot positions along the arc.
  • Labels under the canvas list each slot's binding.

docs.title: 2D fallback
docs.text: On a non-Quest Android device (Cuttlefish, emulator, a phone sideload), the flat preview IS the panel — no AR needed. The same interaction (tap a labeled slot) works.

docs.title: What's not done yet
docs.text:
• Passthrough + hand-tracking driver wiring — see issue #9.
  • Custom slot assignment (drag-drop which panel each slot opens).
  • Per-user arc radius + sweep tuning.

docs.text:

docs.title: Boot Animation panel
docs.text: Swap the Meta startup animation for a nostalgic one (or revert).

docs.title: How Android boot animation works
docs.text:
A specially-named zip at /system/media/bootanimation.zip. Inside: a desc.txt that names play speed + frame directories, plus PNGs in each directory. The AOSP bootanimation binary parses desc.txt and replays frames in order on the primary display at boot.

QuestClassic's swap writes a new zip over that path (after mount -o remount,rw /system), keeps a backup of the original at /data/local/tmp/bootanimation.meta.zip, then remounts read-only.

docs.title: Bundled replacements (all MIT-licensed, clean-room art)
docs.text:
• Classic Oculus Rift CV1 homage — swirling teal orb
  • Terminal Boot — ANSI boot log, green on black
  • QuestClassic Cyan — minimal cyan QC mark, 1.5s loop
  • Dust Particle Field — drifting dust, no text

docs.title: Root gating
docs.text: /system/media/ is read-only on sealed stock. On rooted builds the swap is one remount + copy + chmod. The panel shows the exact commands before running them. See ADR 0009.

docs.title: Revert
docs.text: Picking "Revert to Meta original" writes the backup at /data/local/tmp/bootanimation.meta.zip back over the system file. The backup is created on the first swap and preserved thereafter.

docs.title: Why the backup
docs.text: Meta's bootanimation isn't distributable by us — the frames are Meta IP. The backup is created from the user's own device and kept on the user's own device.

docs.text: • Home menu swapper

docs.title: Build Tools panel
docs.text: A programmable HUD. You pick which widgets to show from a toggle list; chosen widgets render as a stacked column of glass cards. Each widget is small and self-contained — no background work, no services, no persistent state unless the widget explicitly uses DataStore.

docs.title: Shipped widgets
docs.text: Widget Shows Refresh Clock Weekday + HH:MM:SS every 500 ms while visible Fingerprint Build.FINGERPRINT (the full one) static Free memory ActivityManager.MemoryInfo.availMem/totalMem + % every 1.5 s Network ping Resolve + isReachable(2 s) for a user-supplied host on tap Quick note Ephemeral scratch pad (per-session only) — Haptic test Tap-to-buzz every registered BuzzPattern —

docs.title: Adding your own widget
docs.text:
See contributing/getting-started.md and issue #8. Short version:

  1. Open app/src/main/kotlin/io/github/questclassic/app/ui/panels/BuildToolsPanel.kt.
  2. Add a new entry to the Widget enum with a title + a @Composable (AppContainer) -> Unit render lambda.
  3. Write the Composable body.
  4. Done — toggle shows up automatically.

docs.title: Widget rules
docs.text:
• No background services. Use LaunchedEffect + delay scoped to the Composable; rendering pauses the tick.
  • No new manifest permissions without a PR note.
  • No telemetry.
  • One file per widget if it grows past ~60 lines — move to ui/panels/widgets/.
  • No shared state across widgets beyond what AppContainer already exposes.

docs.title: Why a flat enum instead of plugins
docs.text: Widgets are small enough that a class-registry doesn't earn its complexity. An enum entry is the single source of truth: the toggle list, the render switch, the on-disk order. When we hit 20+ widgets or want user-installable third-party widgets we'll revisit; see ADR 0003 for the general philosophy.

docs.title: Future work
docs.text:
• Persist which widgets the user has on (DataStore).
  • Draggable reorder.
  • Widget grid instead of stack.
  • A widget marketplace — issue #8 upgrade.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Developer Super-Mode panel
docs.text: Lifts QuestClassic (and developer-mode settings in general) to capabilities Android normally hides behind extra friction.

docs.title: Toggles
docs.text:
Each toggle names the exact system property or Settings key it flips. Toggle categories:

  • SETTINGS — settings put ...; android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS needed.
  • PROP — setprop ...; needs root or signature permission.
  • PKG — package-level grants (pm grant, appops set).

docs.title: Representative set
docs.text:
• Allow sideload from any source (loosens package-verifier)
  • Full ADB over Wi-Fi without re-pair
  • Keep screen awake while charging
  • Enable layout bounds (overlay layout grid)
  • Allow mock location providers (OpenXR anchor spoofing in tests)
  • Lift SELinux to permissive (temporary; reverse after)
  • Grant QC WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS
  • Grant QC WRITE_SETTINGS
  • Grant QC MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE
  • Disable Meta's device-reset enforcement nag

docs.title: Root gating
docs.text:
PROP toggles need root (or signature-level). PKG toggles need either root or ADB with pm grant — that's a user-performable step. SETTINGS toggles work with WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS already granted (which you get via ADB without root).

So the panel is tiered: PKG + SETTINGS work on any developer-enabled device, PROP toggles need root.

docs.title: Why some of these are dangerous
docs.text:
• setenforce 0 breaks the retail security policy. Reverse it after you're done debugging.
  • MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE lets QC walk any directory; keep it on only when picking firmware files.
  • WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS lets QC flip any Settings.Global key — not just ours.

docs.title: Related
docs.text: • ADR 0009 — Root gating philosophy

docs.title: Diagnostics panel
docs.text: Runs six userspace self-tests and buzzes the controllers in a Morse-like code pattern if any of them fail. Designed to still convey information when the display is unreadable — useful on a headset where vision is the primary output and losing it is the specific problem you most want to diagnose.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text: Test What it measures Fail threshold Buzz pattern Battery BatteryManager.BATTERY_PROPERTY_CAPACITY + BatteryManager.EXTRA_HEALTH <10 % OR health != GOOD -. (BATTERY_LOW) Storage StatFs(/data).availableBytes / totalBytes <5 % free -.. (STORAGE_FULL) RAM ActivityManager.MemoryInfo.lowMemory lowMemory=true no buzz; informational Network NET_CAPABILITY_INTERNET + NET_CAPABILITY_VALIDATED on active network not validated -.-. (WIFI_DOWN) Device Build.MODEL + Build.PRODUCT + SDK n/a — informational — Performance availableProcessors, MemoryInfo.lowMemory as thermal proxy proxy fires -- (THERMAL)

docs.title: How the buzz works
docs.text:
The ControllerHaptics.playPattern(pattern) call constructs a VibrationEffect.createWaveform with alternating on/off timings:

dot     = 80  ms on
dash    = 240 ms on
gap     = 120 ms off (between pulses inside one letter)
longGap = 400 ms off (between letters)
startBurst = 600 ms on, then 400 ms off   ← "pattern incoming" marker

Only the first failed test's pattern is played (otherwise successive buzzes pile up and become un-interpretable). If all tests pass, the OK pattern (...) plays.

docs.title: Reading a pattern you felt
docs.text:
1. Three short pulses back-to-back? Everything's fine, you're good.
  2. One long burst, pause, then a pattern? That's the "pattern incoming" marker — count the dots/dashes that follow.
  3. Match against reference/buzz-patterns.md.

docs.title: UI controls
docs.text:
• Re-run — kicks a fresh pass.
  • Stop buzz — cancels any in-flight vibration. Useful during the Haptic test widget.

docs.title: Why we don't talk to vendor HALs
docs.text: Fine-grained hardware health (eye-tracking LEDs, modem, structured-light projector, depth sensor) lives in vendor HALs under vendor.oculus.hardware.* and vendor.meta.hardware.*. Those are SELinux-gated to signed daemons only; a sideloaded app can't bind to them. The six tests here are what's reachable from unprivileged userspace. That's a real limit, documented honestly — we don't claim to detect something we can't.

docs.title: Related
docs.text:
• reference/buzz-patterns.md — full table.
  • Build Tools → Haptic test — tap-to-feel every pattern on demand.
  • issue #7 — add new patterns via a good first issue.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0.

docs.title: Firmware Dump panel
docs.text: Lists every partition + file a rooted shell could legitimately read off the device, and what you'd get from it. Firmly draws the line at what ISN'T dumpable even with root, and explains why.

docs.title: Dumpable (given root)
docs.text: Target Contents boot_a/_b Linux kernel + ramdisk vendor_boot_a/_b Vendor ramdisk + DTB dtbo_a/_b Device-tree overlay system_a/_b AOSP framework + oculus system apps vendor_a/_b vendor HALs, firmware blobs product_a/_b Meta-specific extras system_ext_a/_b VrShell + oculus system_ext packages otacert Meta's AOSP_Release_Pub-derived OTA cert (public) AVB public keys Chain roots used by vbmeta

docs.title: Partially dumpable
docs.text: Target Why only partial modem_a/_b Raw partition reads; running image lives in QSEE tz_a/_b Partition readable; QSEE won't execute unsigned replacement abl_a/_b Readable, not modifiable without fuse-blow

docs.title: NOT dumpable
docs.text: Target Why OEM PK (per-device) Fuse-rooted; not reachable from software Qualcomm Keybox In TrustZone, no software exfil User biometrics Protected by BiometricPrompt + QSEE

docs.title: What a dump costs
docs.text:
• dd of an A/B system image is ~2 GB on Quest 2. Storage check first.
  • Partition-level dumps write to /sdcard/Dump/ so they're easy to adb pull off.
  • Dumps are reversible-engineerable off-device; the device needs no further privileges to hand them over.

docs.title: Why we can't dump the keys
docs.text: Meta's signing keys, the Qualcomm Keybox, modem firmware, and Adreno GPU microcode all live in silicon fuses or the TrustZone secure world. The hardware is designed specifically to prevent extracting them from software — rooting the normal Android world doesn't change that. See ADR 0009 and firmware-review.md for details.

docs.text:

docs.title: Home Menu Swapper panel
docs.text: Pick what launches when you take the headset off standby.

docs.title: How Android resolves "home"
docs.text:
The intent android.intent.category.HOME is resolved to an Activity. On AOSP Android, first long-press on "home" picks a default; on retail Quest 2 the resolver is hard-wired to com.oculus.shell.

With root, cmd package set-home-activity <pkg>/<Activity> changes the resolution. QuestClassic registers itself as a HOME resolver in its manifest.

docs.title: Candidates
docs.text:
• QuestClassic nostalgic home — this app's own launcher surface
  • QuestClassic AR home — straight into passthrough with the semicircle hand menu
  • Meta VrShell — the stock shell (requires network)
  • Quill (if installed) — "always-on canvas" setup
  • Any sideloaded HOME-category activity — discovered dynamically via PackageManager.queryIntentActivities

docs.title: Root gating
docs.text: Setting the default home activity requires root (to write to /data/system/users/0/home_activity.xml). Without root the panel shows the plan; you can run cmd package set-home-activity ... via ADB as root.

docs.title: Launcher panel
docs.text: A retro-Oculus-style grid of every launchable app on the headset. Taps launch. Tiles are color-coded by whether an app is marked VR-launchable or a regular 2D-panel app.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• VR apps (teal border) — anything that declares com.oculus.intent.category.VR in its manifest. Meta's Store filters and the built-in launcher only surface these in the main Library tab.
  • 2D apps (amber border) — anything with android.intent.category.LAUNCHER. Settings, the Meta Quest Browser, our own app — everything that runs as a 2D panel.
  • Both tags — some apps declare both (Horizon, Store, Settings); we show them as VR.

docs.title: How it finds apps
docs.text:
AppListRepository.load() runs on Dispatchers.IO
  → PackageManager.queryIntentActivities for both intents
  → merge, dedupe by package name, sort by lowercase label

VR-marked packages take precedence; apps found in only the 2D list are tagged 2D.

docs.title: Manifest permission
docs.text: Requires android.permission.QUERY_ALL_PACKAGES. Declared in our manifest; granted automatically on install. Without it we'd only see a few apps on Android 11+.

docs.title: Known limits
docs.text:
• System apps that don't have a launcher intent (DownloadProvider, NetworkStack, etc.) don't show up — correct behavior.
  • "Horizon OS" internal apps sometimes advertise only the VR category and sometimes neither — the launcher reflects what the headset's own launcher would.
  • Icons that are adaptive layered drawables render via a Canvas fallback; occasional apps have no icon at all (we render an empty teal square for those — see AppTile in LauncherPanel.kt).

docs.title: Launching
docs.text: Clicking a tile builds an Intent from the ResolveInfo and calls startActivity with FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK. That's the same mechanism Meta's own launcher uses. If the target app refuses (rare — usually a signed-permission issue), we silently fall through; the tap just doesn't do anything.

docs.title: Future work
docs.text:

  • Pinned / favorites row — not tracked yet; worthy of a good first issue.

docs.title: Meta Hosts Audit panel
docs.text: Resolves + reachability-pings all 24 Meta hosts we identified during the OTA reverse-engineering, grouped into six categories. Educational (shows how Meta's identity / graph / payments fabric stretches across its properties), operational (quick way to spot which Meta service is down), and research (the "Internal" category shouldn't resolve from a consumer device — a surprise there would be investigation-worthy).

docs.title: AUTH (3)
docs.text:
• accountscenter.meta.com — the Meta Accounts Center PWA the AccountsCenter app on-device loads in a WebView.
  • secure.oculus.com — Oculus login endpoint.
  • graph.facebook-hardware.com — the device-auth endpoint (challenge/response, hardware-backed; see reverse-engineering/meta-auth-flow.md).

docs.title: GRAPH (7)
docs.text: Primary GraphQL fabric Meta's apps hit for user data. - graph.oculus.com — Oculus GraphQL (primary). - graph.facebook.com — Facebook main GraphQL — yes, the Oculus apps call it directly, because post-acquisition the account graph is unified. - graph.instagram.com — Instagram GraphQL — only interesting when your Meta account is linked to IG. - b-graph.facebook.com — Facebook bulk GraphQL. - meta.graph.meta.com — Meta-branded GraphQL. - graph-fallback.oculus.com — Oculus GraphQL fallback. - realitylabs-graph.oculus.com — Reality Labs GraphQL.

docs.title: GENAI (2)
docs.text: Meta AI endpoints, baked into retail code paths. - genai-graph.facebook.com - genai-graph.instagram.com

docs.title: PAYMENTS (5)
docs.text: Meta unified-payments GraphQL — same URL template across all Meta properties. - payments-graph.oculus.com - payments-graph.facebook.com - payments-graph.instagram.com - payments-graph.whatsapp.com - payments-graph.graph.meta.com

docs.title: CDN (3)
docs.text:
• scontent.xx.fbcdn.net — Facebook CDN.
  • securecdn.oculus.com — Oculus CDN.
  • rupload.facebook.com — resumable upload.

docs.title: INTERNAL (3)
docs.text: Hosts that appear in the Store/Shell binaries but shouldn't resolve from a consumer device. If one of these ever resolves on YOUR headset, it's worth investigating — it means either Meta's DNS misconfigured, or you're on a Meta-internal network. - graph.intern.facebook.com - m.intern.facebook.com - our.intern.facebook.com

docs.title: How probing works
docs.text:
InetAddress.getByName(host)          ← DNS resolution, short timeout
addr.isReachable(1500ms)             ← ICMP ping or TCP-connect probe

Both run in parallel for all 24 hosts (coroutines + async/awaitAll). Takes about 2 seconds total on a decent Wi-Fi.

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text:
Each host card shows:

  • IP address (if DNS resolved).
  • Latency (if the ping succeeded — typical ~50-200 ms from US Wi-Fi).
  • "unreachable" (DNS resolved, ping failed — common on networks that block ICMP; the host may still be TCP-443 reachable).
  • DNS fail / error message (if resolution itself failed — expected for *.intern.facebook.com).

The top of each group shows X/Y reachable.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text: The panel only resolves and pings. Meta sees the DNS query (at your DNS resolver, not at Meta's edge unless they operate it) and an ICMP echo. No authentication, no account identifier, nothing from your user profile leaves the device via this panel.

docs.title: Why 24 hosts specifically
docs.text:
Harvested from the DEX strings of every Meta-online APK and from libshell.so's .rodata section during the reverse-engineering (see reverse-engineering/hosts-glossary.md). If Meta adds more endpoints in future builds, we'll learn them from a new OTA analysis and extend the list.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0 + the 2026-09-06 Quest 2 OTA.

docs.title: Functionality Restore panel
docs.text: Option 9 from the design brief: the "post / hardware check" escalation ladder.

docs.title: The ladder
docs.text:
1. Ask — "Do you notice any problems?" with a 30s timer.
  2. Attempt fix — on no-answer or yes:
  3. Recalibrate tracking origin
  4. Re-bind controllers
  5. Re-query displays
  6. Run self-tests — if the fix attempt doesn't reveal the problem, run the full diagnostics engine.
  7. Display error — if a failing check is found, show its name + value on screen.
  8. Fallback text — if the main display surface is unreachable (compositor dead), show the error code on a plain fallback surface.
  9. Buzz — if nothing can be rendered, buzz the controllers and headset in the pattern tied to the finding.

docs.title: Buzz pattern lookup
docs.text: Each diagnostic code maps to a canonical pattern in docs/reference/buzz-patterns.md. Users can decode a fault by feeling the pattern and matching it in the public repo.

docs.title: Why 30 seconds
docs.text: A user who is trying the headset for the first time — or has just had one go wrong — needs time to look, feel, and consider before pressing. Short enough to respect their time, long enough not to race past them.
