docs.title: Signature Verifier panel
docs.text: Pick a Meta OTA .zip from Downloads; the panel reproduces the exact two signature checks the Quest bootloader does at install time, offline and on-device.

docs.title: Why
docs.text: So that any user can confirm, from their own headset, that an OTA archive was really signed by Meta and hasn't been modified. The bootloader does this before applying; we do it on demand so you can verify an archive you got from somewhere other than Meta's official update server.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
An AOSP A/B update_engine payload (the payload.bin inside the OTA) has two independent RSA-2048 + SHA-256 signatures:

  1. Metadata signature — covers bytes [0 .. 24 + manifest_size) (the CrAU header + the DeltaArchiveManifest).
  2. Final payload signature — covers [0 .. 24 + manifest_size) ∪ [data_blobs_start .. final_sig_at) — header + manifest + data blobs. The metadata signature bytes are skipped — they aren't persisted to disk during install (AOSP quirk; this trips up most first-time verifiers).

Both signatures are RSA-2048 over a PKCS#1 v1.5 + DigestInfo-wrapped SHA-256. Verified with Java's Signature.getInstance("NONEwithRSA") against the public key extracted from the OTA's own META-INF/com/android/otacert.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text:
1. Tap Pick OTA.
  2. Android's file picker opens — navigate to Downloads, pick the .zip.
  3. The app reads just payload.bin and otacert.pem from the ZIP (streamed — no full extraction even on a 1 GB payload), computes the two digests, verifies.
  4. Result card tells you valid/invalid for each signature plus:
  5. Payload header values (size, manifest size, metadata-sig size, final-sig offset)
  6. Both SHA-256 digests (so you can compare against a separate reference, e.g. tools/verify_payload.py)
  7. OTA cert subject, issuer, not-after, SHA-256 fingerprint

docs.title: What a passing verify proves
docs.text:
• The archive was signed by the holder of the private key that pairs with the public cert in the archive.
  • Not a single byte of payload.bin has been modified since the signer signed it.

It does NOT prove:

  • That the signer is actually Meta (unless you compare the cert fingerprint against Meta's known one — the canonical SHA-256 is B8:C9:D2:8A:61:6F:83:14:85:C2:3F:13:6D:AB:91:B0:91:C9:9A:A0:3D:CA:57:08:1A:25:D1:4F:3B:C1:9F:A1, matching CN=AOSP_Release_Pub, O=Oculus).
  • That the OTA will install on your device (anti-rollback / device allow-list are separate checks the bootloader makes).

docs.title: Native port of the Python tool
docs.text:
This panel is a straight Kotlin reimplementation of tools/verify_payload.py. The Kotlin version is behaviorally identical — same byte ranges, same PKCS#1 v1.5 handling, same manifest-skipping trick for the final signature — and shares zero code with the Python version (the Python is pure stdlib; Kotlin uses Java crypto).

If a verification mysteriously succeeds on one and fails on the other, that's a bug; open an issue with both outputs attached.

docs.title: Strip Meta panel
docs.text: Dry-run plan + root-gated action for debloating a Quest 2 of Meta-origin packages.

docs.title: What you see
docs.text:
A card per Meta-origin package, tagged with the planned verb:

  • REMOVE (green) — uninstall at user 0. Safe to remove; does not block boot.
  • DISABLE (amber) — pm disable-user; removable in theory but used by system intents, so disabling keeps intents resolvable.
  • LEAVE (red) — removing it blanks the compositor, tracking, or launcher. The app will not propose removing these.

Each entry shows the exact shell command that would run. Even on a stock headset the plan is useful as documentation.

docs.title: Root gating
docs.text:
The top of the panel displays a RootGateCard describing what QuestClassic detected about the device's root state. See ADR 0009 for why we detect-but-never-exploit.

On stock retail firmware, the destructive action is a no-op: you can read the plan and run the commands yourself via ADB if you choose.

docs.title: System Internals panel
docs.text: The deep-reading version of the About panel. Surfaces, live on the headset, every fingerprint and quirk our reverse-engineering turned up — categorized, cross-linked, and highlighted when something's worth paying attention to.

docs.title: OS lineage
docs.text:
Pulled from getprop:

  • ro.product.system.model + ro.product.system.manufacturer
  • ro.product.system.device (codename — hollywood on Quest 2)
  • ro.build.branch — the real HorizonOS version, like releases-oculus-14.0-v209. Android's version string (14.0) is just the AOSP base, not the HorizonOS release.
  • ro.build.version.release, .sdk, ro.product.first_api_level
  • ro.vndk.version
  • ro.oculus.reality_mode — mr on Quest 2 regardless of whether MR is active

docs.title: Security patch gap
docs.text:
Compares ro.build.version.security_patch against ro.vendor.build.security_patch. If they differ, the panel highlights the row in amber and explains: common Qualcomm-vendor anti-pattern — the vendor partition carries its own SPL which is often months-to-years behind the user-facing patch level. Qualcomm BSP patches between those dates may not be reflected in this build.

On the Quest 2 OTA we analysed in 2026:

  • device-wide SPL: 2026-09-06
  • vendor partition SPL: 2018-06-05

An 8-year gap.

docs.title: Build-host leak
docs.text:
ro.build.host and ro.system.build.fingerprint sometimes carry internal build-server hostnames that Meta's release pipeline didn't scrub. On the Nov 2026 Quest 2 build:

3c64-a274-15de-0a00.twshared10220.29.lla2.tw.fbinfra.net

Decoded:

  • twshared — Meta's Tupperware (internal container platform)
  • lla2 — Luleå, Sweden datacenter 2
  • fbinfra.net — Facebook/Meta internal infra DNS zone
  • The hex-looking first segment is the container/machine ID

If this string is present on your device, the panel flags it amber. It's not a security vulnerability — it's a soft information leak Meta likely intended to scrub.

docs.title: SoC + GPU
docs.text:
• ro.soc.manufacturer, ro.soc.model (Qualcomm SM8250 on Quest 2 — the base for Snapdragon XR2 Gen 1)
  • ro.hardware.egl, ro.hardware.vulkan (Adreno on Quest)
  • ro.bionic.cpu_variant (cortex-a55 — the lowest-common across SM8250's big.LITTLE cluster)
  • ro.product.cpu.abilist
  • A/B + dynamic partitions + virtual A/B flags

docs.title: USB + recovery
docs.text:
• ro.recovery.usb.vid — 2833 is Meta's USB vendor ID
  • ro.recovery.usb.adb.pid, .fastboot.pid — Quest 2 PIDs are 0086 and 0081
  • ro.zygote — Quest 2 is still zygote32, meaning apps run 32-bit by default (!)

docs.title: Why these specific highlights
docs.text: Each one came out of the OTA reverse-engineering done before we wrote this app. The full write-up is in reverse-engineering/overview.md and the parent project's RE report.

docs.title: What's intentionally NOT here
docs.text:
• Nothing that requires elevated permissions (we don't have them).
  • Nothing from vendor HALs (SELinux-gated; see Diagnostics § Why we don't talk to vendor HALs).
  • Nothing that would require executing a binary with elevated privileges.

Last reviewed against v0.1.0 + the 2026-09-06 Quest 2 OTA.

docs.title: Updates panel
docs.text: Polls this repo's GitHub Releases for a newer version, offers to download and install the newer APK through Android's standard PackageInstaller.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
onOpen:
  GET https://api.github.com/repos/A-Hackers-Guide/QuestClassic/releases/latest
    ← JSON {tag_name, name, assets: [{name, browser_download_url, size}]}
  compare tag_name vs BuildConfig.VERSION_NAME (semver-ish)
  if newer AND release has an .apk asset:
    show "Install" button
  else:
    show "You're on the latest."

Tap "Install":

download asset → cacheDir/questclassic-update.apk
launch ACTION_VIEW with the FileProvider URI
  → Android PackageInstaller UI
  → user confirms → app updates, re-opens on new version

docs.title: First install needs one permission
docs.text: REQUEST_INSTALL_PACKAGES. The first time you tap Install, Android pops the system "Allow Install unknown apps" setting; grant it to QuestClassic in Settings → Apps → Install unknown apps → QuestClassic. One-time.

docs.title: What's hard-coded vs rewritten at release time
docs.text:
SelfUpdater.kt ships with:

const val OWNER = "REPLACE_WITH_OWNER"
const val REPO = "QuestClassic"

release.yml runs sed to replace both with the actual owner/repo at build time. So a fork of this project gets its own update channel for free — it polls its own release feed, not ours.

docs.title: Why GitHub, not Meta's OTA pipeline
docs.text:
• We can't sign a Meta OTA. The signing chain is rooted in a key in Meta's HSM; see reverse-engineering/avb-chain.md.
  • Even if we could, pushing to Meta's OTA pipeline requires Meta infrastructure.
  • Meta's OTAs don't wipe user-installed APKs on A/B updates, so our channel coexists with theirs peacefully. The headset's HorizonOS gets updated by Meta; QuestClassic gets updated by us; neither interferes.

See ADR 0005 for the full reasoning.

docs.title: Semver comparison
docs.text: SelfUpdater.compareSemver strips a leading v, splits on . and -, and compares component-by-component. So v0.2.0-rc.1 > v0.1.0 and v1.0.0 > v0.99.0. Non-numeric components are treated as 0 (e.g. v1.0.0-alpha and v1.0.0-beta compare equal — we don't currently distinguish). Good enough for v0; issue #12 has a note to add a real semver comparator with tests.

docs.title: Network footprint
docs.text:
Two hosts in total:

  • api.github.com — one HTTPS GET per panel open.
  • github.com — one HTTPS GET when downloading an asset.

No analytics. No ping. No "anonymous usage telemetry." See security/model.md for the complete list of network endpoints the app can reach.
